speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker.
I am sorry that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Chretien) is not here, but as a member of this house and a French Canadian, I must protest against the fact that officials of the Department of National Revenue are sending me 1967 income tax forms in English only, addressed as follows:
Master Real Caouette
Parliament House
Ottawa
I even wonder if the official in question did not deliberately send me that form in English only in an envelope also endorsed entirely in English:
Taxation Data Center
P.O. Box 456
Ottawa 2, Ontario
Mr Speaker, I protest against this fact, and I think it is a question of privilege, because last year, I asked the department to send French forms to French speaking people in the province of Quebec. I was then told that errors had been made.
I maintain that no English speaking member would accept to receive a French income tax form, and I have the right to pay my federal taxes in French, Mr. Speaker.

BROADCASTING

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, January 22, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-163, to implement a broadcasting policy for Canada, to amend the Radio Act in consequence thereof and to enact other consequential and related provisions-Miss LaMarsh- Mr. Batten in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: BROADCASTING
speechtext:
When the committee rose on Monday, January 22, clause 2 of the bill was under consideration together with an amendment thereto proposed by the hon. member for Lapointe.
On clause 2-Broadcasting policy for Canada.

maintopic: BROADCASTING
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at ten o'clock last night when I was discussing clause 2 of the bill before us I read from a letter addressed to Dr. Andrew Stewart, chairman of the Board of Broadcast Governors in Ottawa, written on December 5, 1966, by the operators of the C.A.T.V. broadcasting installation at Wawa. I read the major portion of the letter pointing out the tremendous expenditures that these people had made on behalf of the C.A.T.V. subscribers in Wawa. I should like at this time to complete the reading of the letter. It continues as follows:
Should such authority be withheld, we shall have no alternative but to terminate our operation, incur a substantial loss on our investment in that community and deprive the residents of Wawa alternative TV programs which they have enjoyed for the past eight years, due only to the painstaking efforts on the part of our company which have brought us some really insignificant monetary rewards.

I should perhaps point out that there are at present approximately 1,000 dwellings in the town of Wawa and that we are serving 800 of these.
We hope and expect that when the application made to the Department of Transport by Northern Telephone Limited, for authority to discontinue the reception and relay of programs from station CJIC-TV Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, and to replace them with the programs of station WWTV-TV channel 10 Cadillac, Michigan, when the proposed C.B.C. television rebroadcasting station at Wawa, Ontario begins scheduled operation, that you will take account of the facts herein above stated, and that you will see your way clear, in view of the special circumstances of our situation and that of the Wawa residents, to give favourable consideration to Northern's application.
Should you require any further information, I am of course entirely at your disposal.
Yours very truly, Gilbert A. Allard
This letter pointed out the situation existing in Wawa when the people in that town wished to bring in programs from Cadillac and Traverse City, Michigan, instead of from the Sault Ste. Marie station whenever the C.B.C. rebroadcasting station should start operating in Wawa itself.
I have in my hand a copy of a letter from J. R. Baldwin, deputy minister of transport, dated March 23, 1967, rejecting the application of Northern Telephone Limited. It reads as follows:
Your application dated June 24, 1966 for authority to replace the programs of station CJIC-TV Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario with those of station WWTV-TV Cadillac-Traverse City, Mich., at your land station performing a commercial broadcasting receiving service at Montreal River, Ontario, for relay via your authorized microwave system to subscribers at Wawa, Ontario, has been considered in accordance with the minister's announcement in the House of Commons on July 22, 1964. The Board of Broadcast Governors has advised the minister that it does not support the application submitted by your company.
The application of Northern Telephone Company Limited having been turned down to bring in programs from Cadillac on an authorized microwave transmission system between Sault Ste. Marie and Wawa, there is now a C.A.T.V. installation in Wawa which is offering the people there the opportunity to look at programs from the Sault Ste. Marie station which is a C.B.C. affiliate while on the second channel on their C.A.T.V. dial they can look at C.B.C. programs coming from the rebroadcasting station opened by the C.B.C. in Wawa in December, 1967, or else they can get an indistinct picture of programs coming from Marquette, Michigan. I do not know of any other place in Canada where a C.A.T.V. operator has been given permission to bring
January 23, 1968

in the same program on two different channels to one community. This is absolutely ridiculous on the face of it, and I can see no defence for it whatsoever.
As I mentioned last night, the B.B.G. must have given my respected friend, the Secretary of State, a high-sounding explanation when they stated that the application of Northern Telephone Limited to drop the Sault Ste. Marie station from its existing system at Wawa in favour of the channel emanating from Cadillac, Michigan, was rejected because the board felt the system should carry the available Canadian channel. Under these terms it is a marvel that they do not state that Canadian television viewers can only have one channel on their receiving sets so that they will not be given the opportunity of playing with the dial and receiving more than one program.
Here we have the same program being brought into Wawa by two different methods and the C.A.T.V. operators are told they cannot replace one of the two similar Canadian programs with an alternative United States program because the B.B.G. does not favour it. I said yesterday and I repeat again that if someone can show me any sense in that reasoning I wish they would give it to me in detail for I feel certain I could not understand any explanation that may be advanced to support the ruling rejecting the application of the Northern Telephone Company to bring in a United States station. I was reading in some detail yesterday the explanation provided by the Secretary of State for the rejection in the year ended March 31, 1967, of seven C.A.T.V. applications by the B.B.G. I made myself clear that I am indebted to her for her full report on the seven applications that were turned down by the B.B.G. On the other hand, the Minister of Transport, within whose field these applications came, gave no reason at all for the rejection of the applications.

I would be remiss in my duty if I did not make some comments about several speeches which we were privileged to hear or burdened with listening to-it depends on how you look at it-yesterday. Some of the speeches, to say the least, I found amazing. I am referring to the speeches made by the hon. members for Elgin and Red Deer. I congratulate the hon. member for Elgin on his wide-ranging speech which demonstrated to me that he had excellent technical assistance, as good as the assistance provided to cabinet ministers in Canadian governments by their executive assistants. In his criticism of the C.B.C. the hon. member for Elgin dealt with C.B.C. reporting of race problems in the United States, C.B.C. coverage of United States foreign policy and C.B.C. coverage of domestic politics in the United States. I find it hard to believe that any Canadian member of parliament who looks after his constituency and tries to follow legislation and estimates in the house, which must be followed and dealt with, has been able to find the time to become as knowledgeable about United States
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting affairs as the hon. member for Elgin seems to be.
The hon. member for Elgin has just left the chamber. I am sorry because I do not like to criticize an hon. member who is not here. Since he was here when I began speaking I shall continue. There is nothing wrong with that. The hon. member for Elgin may agree with Mr. Zink. If the hon. member for Elgin did not have Mr. Zink's assistance in preparing his speech I can only conclude that two people in Canada have identical views on almost any subject one can think of.

I do not agree with this proposal. Moreover, I should like to say to the hon. members that either they have forgotten or they simply do not know what their own party in years gone by felt about this issue and what every government since the thirties has felt about it.
I want to remind hon. members to my right that it was a Conservative prime minister, Mr. Bennett, who said when the C.B.C. was established that Canadians had a right to a system of broadcasting from Canadian sources equal to that of any other country and that Canada must be assured of complete control of broadcasting from Canadian sources free from any interference. One cannot achieve these things which Mr. Bennett commended so eloquently in the absence of a publicly owned television system. I certainly hope and expect that the government will ignore the proposals which have been made so frequently by the official opposition that the corporation should be disposed of or its activities curtailed.
In the few minutes which remain to me I should like to deal with what I believe to be an important subject, a field which has been virtually ignored. I refer to the activities of private radio stations. When television began to develop in Canada in 1952 or thereabouts many people thought that radio stations would virtually disappear because people would no longer listen to them. Since that time nobody has been paying much attention to the affairs of the radio stations.
The fact is that the radio stations of Canada have never been so numerous, so affluent and so successful in securing advertising revenue as they are today. There seems to be no end to their growth. I have no objection to this. In 1952 there were 169 privately owned radio stations. In 1965 there were 281 such stations; that figure includes both a.m. and f.m. stations. It is true that television secured the lion's share of the total broadcasting revenue in 1965, the last year for which C.B.S. figures are available, but radio stations took in more than $70 million or some 42 per cent of total broadcastig revenues. Each year the sale of radio receivers exceeds that of television sets.
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting That radio broadcasting is a profitable business is obvious if one studies the figures to be found, for example, in the Financial Post. One sees that the corporation called Selkirk Holdings, which owns radio stations in Lethbridge, Edmonton, Calgary, Hamilton, Victoria, Vancouver and elsewhere, has increased its profits in each of the past three years, that Standard Radio, which owns stations in Toronto and Montreal, has similarly increased its profits every year, that Western Broadcasting, which has stations in Vancouver and elsewhere, has similarly seen its profits increase. Everything I say today will represent entirely my own thinking and interpretation in respect of this matter. I agree that private members of the house do not have the research facilities which when used sometimes result in long tedious speeches, and that they do not is perhaps best for all concerned.
I enter this debate mainly because during the Christmas recess, as I presume was the case with most hon. members, I was called to many meetings in my constituency. We had been away for a long time sitting almost continually here in the House of Commons. There were many matters which constituents wished to discuss with their members as a result of that long absence. This applies mainly to those of us from the more distant parts of Canada who do not have an opportunity to keep as closely in touch with our constituencies as those who live closer at hand.
I found a strong wave of protest across the country on many matters. In fact I have never attended so many protest meetings in all my years in the house. I can tell the government there are many unhappy citizens across this nation in respect of many policies or lack of policies. No doubt those who were in the central part of Canada during the week end when the leadership candidates were there were made aware of this spirit of protest personally during their sojourn in the city of Winnipeg.
The one meeting I attended relating to the particular subject before the committee at the
5854	COMMONS DEBATES
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting moment was convened by a committee in the city of Brandon which calls itself the committee for better broadcasting. I, along with other interested citizens, met with this committee for a period of some four hours. In fact the meeting went on until midnight and would not have broken up at that hour had there not been the problem of time. I discovered that this committee, which actually had been formed to protest monopoly broadcasting in southwestern Manitoba, in reality was more concerned about the quality of broadcasting than any other subject. This was a spontaneous protest which arose following the recent hearings before the B.B.G. with regard to a second channel television service in southwestern Manitoba.
The committee was formed for the purpose of opposing any extension of monopoly in broadcasting. In response to a newspaper advertisement some 4,000 citizens communicated with the B.B.G. to express their feelings on this important subject. As I say, while the main item of concern was monopoly broadcasting, both radio and television, it turned out at the meeting I attended that the citizens were more concerned about the quality of broadcasting by both the private broadcasters and the C.B.C.
It is not necessary for me to enlarge on some of the matters which were brought before that meeting. In the interest of brevity I should add that the following day the chairman of the B.B.G., Dr. Stewart, arrived in the city of Brandon. A special meeting of the board was convened at which the board was represented by Mrs. Sweatman and the chairman. During that board meeting the members of the board were subjected to a repetition of the experience which had been mine on the previous evening. Therefore, without bringing the matters before the house in detail I can assure the responsible minister and members of the committee that the B.B.G. has been fully informed concerning the problem.
I do not know whether this was an exceptional circumstances in Canadian broadcasting affairs but I do know that there is a very enlightened electorate in the Brandon-Souris constituency. I would imagine that other members have had similar experiences, if not before a special committee, at least through correspondence and other forms of communication. I want to emphasize that the quality of broadcasting both by the C.B.C. and by private radio and television services is of great and growing concern to the people in southwestern Manitoba.

January 23, 1968
It is natural that there should be this type of public reaction because broadcasting both television and radio, is a comparatively new facility in the area of communication and as electronic mass media they are having a growing impact on the thinking of the people and therefore on the public policy of the nation. Even though we have had broadcasting for a comparatively short space of time, actually just over a quarter of a century, we know what can be accomplished by the skilful use of this mass media.
Mass media is a vital and integral part of the whole modern process of brainwashing which is a part of our psychological stock in trade today. While the hidden persuaders still use the printed word, to a growing extent I would say that they are resorting to mass media in order to engage in subtle forms of hidden persuasion at the subliminal level which motivate much of our way of life today. In the political area we have the example of what took place in nazi Germany where a monstrous authoritarian regime was able to maintain control. In addition to removing the normal processes of parliamentary democracy they were actually able to obtain the support of the masses by_ manipulation through the skilful use of radio broadcasting. We are all aware that President Roosevelt for many years was able to maintain a strong influence over the electorate in the United States even though most of the major newspapers of that country were opposed to his policies. He was able to do this through his fireside chats. Through his skilful use of broadcasting he maintained this influence over the people of the United States.

I am sure his exposure through the means of television is going to have considerable influence and impact on his contemplated political career. I do not want to pursue this thought further, and if I am going to maintain my vow of brevity I must move to the next point.
There have been criticisms that C.B.C. broadcasting policy and private broadcasting activities have a less than desirable influence on our Canadian society. I am inclined to agree with that because the mass media does reflect a trend toward increasing urbanization in Canada. I served on the broadcasting committee away back when-a long time ago. One of the points I repeatedly brought before the committee was that in C.B.C. programming local interests are not represented. Most of the programs originate from big metropolitan communities such as Montreal and Toronto, and to a lesser extent Winnipeg and Vancouver, with the result that inevitably there is going to be an influence reflecting the process of urbanization in this country, and urban influence is a secular influence. It is a materialistic and often sensuous influence. Anyone who has visited the C.B.C. broadcasting centres in Toronto and Montreal soon discovers that gathered there are groups of artists and programmers who are completely caught up in the secular urban trend under way throughout the entire western world.
Someone referred to what Oswald Spangler said in his writings after world war I, that the inevitable drift from a predominantly rural society to a secularized, industrialized, urban society will bring about drastic changes

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting in values. It is this trend that several members have protested against during the course of the general discussion at the committee stage.
There is very little spiritual or religious influence in mass media communications at the present time. This not only applies to the arena of broadcasting but to all our other social institutions as well. Someone has said that the only spiritual uplift modern man is capable of today is that which he derives from the pursuit of the cocktail circuit where he becomes filled with spirit and as a result enters into new dimensions. We might also add to that the resort to pills, sexual thrills, and all the other things which are part of the western urbanization of today. This trend applies to all the other social institutions as well.
It is for this reason, I am sure, that the late Governor General Vanier felt compelled to establish the Vanier Institute of the Family. He was aware that this basic social institution was being profoundly eroded by the secular drift that is under way in our so-called western civilization. Perhaps this is not the time to refer to this, Mr. Chairman, but very shortly we will be debating amendments to the Criminal Code, just as we have recently debated divorce reforms. This indicates that the family as a social institution today is no longer the healing place of the soul as it used to be in more stable times. It is the breeding ground for divorce and delinquency. This is the important point which was brought to our attention by the Vanier Institute of the Family. Anyone who has read the recent writings of Dr. Wilder Penfield will quickly come to the conclusion that these are the problems which concern him. Our mass media of communication as well as the basic social institutions have come under the influence of the inevitable drift toward a secular, urban society.
If time allowed I could deal with education as well because changes are taking place in our educational system. In the old Victorian days, referred to I think by the hon. member for Winnipeg North, it used to be reading, writing and arithmetic that were taught. This apparently has been changed by the addition of another category. It is now reading, writing, arithmetic and rioting. There is a great protest emanating from our educational institutions at all levels. I am sure hon. members noted the recent caustic comments of Malcolm Muggeridge who resigned as chancellor of the University of Edinburgh, one of the most
January 23, 1968


demonstrated forcefully by the chairman of the board, Dr. Stewart, who came all the way out to Manitoba just two weeks ago, bringing with him the Manitoba representative on the board, to see for himself the reasons for the protests that had arisen in southwestern Manitoba. I trust that the new regulatory body, the C.R.C., will have the same interest and zeal in pursuing a more excellent course for broadcasting. I am sure it will if Dr. Stewart and those who have been associated with him in the past are retained on that board. I am quite optimistic concerning these matters. I am not too concerned that sometimes local, private broadcasting stations abuse their privileges. We all abuse our privileges; it is the nature of homo sapiens, sometimes referred to as homo the sap. But eventually there is a reaction and we And the citizens deciding for themselves that all is not for the best. Then they take the initiative and eventually the quality of broadcasting is elevated. As a result the quality of life as manifest through mass media communication is raised accordingly.

Mr. Chairman, toward the end of his remarks, the previous speaker, if I understood him correctly, quoted Malcolm Muggeridge as being somewhat disillusioned with the youth of today who, according to Mr. Muggeridge-at least, I understood Mr. Muggeridge was being quoted and they were not the words of the hon. member-are concerned more with sex and pot and not with the finer things with which they were concerned in Mr. Muggeridge's day. I take issue with Mr. Muggeridge on this question. I think what we are in fact witnessing today, which is perhaps in some degree reflected on radio and television, is a much more open society in which there is a greater opportunity for a far greater number of people to express themselves both intelligently and unintelligently. Sometimes, therefore, in reference to mass media, particularly television, people are upset when they hear views expressed which are not their own. I believe that if television is to be a meaningful instrument in society this trend will continue rather than diminish because television must reflect the changes that are taking place in our modern society.
Another factor that I think we find upsetting about the mass media is that in the period 50 or 60 years ago or whenever it was-I suppose it was not that long ago-that Mr. Muggeridge was talking about the world of ideas was limited to those who had education
January 23, 1968

and they were relatively much smaller in number than is the case today. It was limited to those who had access to books. I think we would find among the intellectual community, if that is the correct term, of 50 years ago as much depravity as we find among the intellectual community today. I do not know that the morals of the intellectual community, if one can find such a community, have really changed in the last 50 years.
Perhaps what has changed more than anything else is that we have become more democratic and the average citizen is able to be exposed more to all facets of life and has a little more time to pursue the finer as well as the not so fine aspects of life. I believe this trend is being expressed in one form or another on the mass media. There is a certain group of people in our society who have preconceived notions of how it must operate. These rules are not always applied to themselves because the alteration of that sort of strict code can be permitted for the few. But if there is any danger that the masses may indulge in the same way of life this, of course, can be upsetting.
To put it another way, I think our criticism of the mass media is sometimes more the result of uncertainty about the consequences of the changes we are experiencing. Naturally, television as a mass media must be part of this picture. I suppose it can be said that when there is an unknown quantity many people may be concerned. Perhaps there are those who, while they may argue on the one hand that this trend is good because it is democratic and open, say that in fact television as a mass medium can be used by a particular group which has a particular philosophy about society to exploit or perhaps unduly influence society. Therefore I suppose one of the real dangers in the policy of broadcasting is an imbalance in this connection. A proper balance must be maintained.
I think it is safe to say that up until now there has been an imbalance in this area. I do not think the reactionaries of the country feel they have the same opportunity of expression as others. I do not know whether they have; I have not monitored all the programs. However, I suppose it may be said that some of the views allowed to be expressed on the mass media tend to be what may generally be regarded as the more progressive and sometimes we do not hear enough of other, more reactionary views. I suppose that in all fairness there ought to be some kind of balance and there is undoubtedly therefore, at least

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting theoretically, a danger present in the broadcasting media.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
While the issue of broadcasting has been with us since the beginning of broadcasting and will continue to be with us, I think that what we are in fact talking about is society itself and how the mass media reflect it. My particular reason for speaking in the debate today is to deal with two matters that are of concern to me. One has to do with public broadcasting policy with regard to the extension of service. I am concerned about the fact that in the development of broadcasting in this country-and I intend to go along with some of the things that the hon. member for Brandon-Souris said in this regard-there is a danger that the large metropolitan centres will control the mass media more and more to the detriment of some of the other regions of Canada.
We all recognize, I believe, that it is in the larger centres that the greater opportunities exist for people in the arts who would like to have their talents displayed on television. But at the same time I feel that in viewing the policy of the Canadian broadcasting system there is reason for the valid criticism that over the years the C.B.C. has not always and at all times adhered strictly enough to the view that one of its primary functions is the extension of service. I know that certainly a great deal has been done in this area, but in 1968 we find that a great many Canadians still do not enjoy the modern advantages of television. So it is a little annoying to these people to hear about large expenditures and great public buildings going up while at the same time they do not enjoy the benefits of a service.
Let us take my own province as an example. One of the things for which the former member representing Burin-Burgeo fought during his entire period as a member of the house was public broadcasting in his constituency. To this day there is no public radio broadcasting in his constituency although there are two private radio stations which operate there. The same goes for television, although in the case of television the private broadcasters at that time did not have a station in the province of Newfoundland. However, in the case of the south coast of Newfoundland, the example of the initiative of private enterprise vis-a-vis the C.B.C. is a telling one and warrants criticism. The same situation still exists today so far as television is concerned in my own constituency which is
January 23, 1988

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting never more than 100 miles at any point from the city of St. John's. There are a number of areas there which do not enjoy television coverage, and this is even more true of other areas in Newfoundland.
The second matter which I believe has regional overtones concerns the policy of public broadcasting so far as the development of Canada on a regional level is concerned. Again I think the C.B.C. is faced with a serious problem in this respect because there are only so many dollars to be spent and there are a great many ways to spend them. At the same time, those of us who come from the periphery of Canada and do not live in the great metropolitan centres have more than a legitimate complaint that too much of public broadcasting is controlled from these centres. This is bad for a number of reasons. It is bad because it reduces the opportunity for a number of people to participate. Therefore in a quantitative sense it is unfortunate. Second, it has a qualitative effect because if public broadcasting is concentrated, as it is, in one or two large metropolitan centres it is more difficult to achieve the diversity which could be obtained if there were greater autonomy or greater opportunities at the regional level.
I believe there is a relationship between culture, art, drama and geography. The hon. member for Essex South mentioned fog. Although he may never have seen it physically he should have more knowledge of it in a metaphysical sense than most hon. members in the house. I would have thought the hon. member for Essex South would share my views because I would not think that Windsor is one of the great metropolitan centres of this country.
The qualitative effects to which I referred are due to the fact that, as I said, culture, art and drama are related to geography. Therefore I believe that a greater emphasis should be placed upon the development of talent in regions other than the metropolitan centres. It is not solely the responsibility of television to undertake the development of talent. Opportunities can be provided in many ways. However, I feel that television must play an important role. I was pleased to note last night that the C.B.C. broadcast a program which originated from St. John's, Newfoundland. I am sure that those hon. members who did not see that program will have heard about it because there are few parts of Canada as rich in folklore and culture as the province of Newfoundland, unless it be the province of Quebec. I contratulate the C.B.C. for its production last night. However, I think
[Mr. Cashin.I
that greater emphasis should be placed in the future on the development of talent in the Atlantic provinces and also on providing opportunities for the development of talent in western Canada. Not only would this be justified on the basis that it opens the media to more people but also because it can have a qualitative as well as a quantitative effect. Not only will new people be brought in but I believe that people from the different regions of Canada will have an effect on the quality of the programs.
There are certain attitudes or certain factors which may perhaps make for a greater diversity in programming. Obviously one of the facts of life in Canada is our regional and cultural diversity, and I think the C.B.C. has a role to play in its development. We speak a great deal about national unity. I hope that national unity does not mean we should all become the same and, so far as television is concerned, become more and more like those who live in Toronto or Montreal. It would be a great advantage to Canada, not only so far as television is concerned but in many other areas, if greater opportunities were given to people in the more distant areas of Canada.
Let me refer to the program "Viewpoint" as an illustration of the policy. It so happens that very seldom do we see people from the Atlantic provinces appearing on that program. I have made some inquiries, not official but quite informal ones, and it would be safe to say that the C.B.C. has had some difficulties in using people from the Atlantic provinces on that program. This was the impression I received. If this is the case, then I think it is a reflection on the efforts of the C.B.C. and perhaps more than anything else it spells out an attitude of mind that may lead us to believe that Canada extends from York on one side to Humber on the other.

part of our country. There are some who may not think so but, although there are only 100,000 people in Prince Edward Island, in a qualitative sense the population of that island and their way of life enrich this country. Mr. Chairman, I should like first of all to commend the hon. member for St. John's West for the first part of his speech. I did not mind the last part and all that blarney that we listened to, but in the first part of his speech he pointed out what I think was a modern point of view about morals and life today compared with the point of view expressed by the hon. member for Bran-don-Souris and others. I should like to say a few words about this question.
Before I do so, Mr. Chairman, I have in front of me the white paper on broadcasting, 1966, prepared by the House of Commons standing committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts. I notice that it was presented to the house on March 21, 1967. I am one of those who were active members of the broadcasting committee. I sat through almost every minute of its hearings when the committee was reviewing the white paper, when the bill was drafted and sent back to the committee for review, and again in the house I have listened to almost every minute of the debate.
I have restrained myself from speaking for most of the time but it now seems to me that if we get through this broadcasting bill by June we will be doing rather well. I have come to the conclusion that it is rather pointless for me to sit here listening as the debate goes on to many things with which I disagree and to continue to remain silent. Therefore I
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting am going to make a small contribution at this time. Perhaps the first anniversary of the report or the bill will soon be reached and we shall still be debating this subject.
At this point I want to refer in particular to a theme which has come up in the speeches of a number of members. I refer to the speech made before the Christmas adjournment by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke. I also noticed the same theme in the speech of the hon. member for Kinders-ley, in the speech of the hon. member for Rosthern, in the speech of the hon. member for Acadia, and particularly in the speech made yesterday by the hon. member for Red Deer. These speeches had to do with, I suppose, morality or morals in broadcasting.
I think the hon. member for Brandon-Sou-ris referred to the sensuous quality of broadcasts, that sort of thing which is perhaps related to the kind of thing the hon. member for Acadia referred to earlier in his speech, the type of scenes that he may have viewed in some programs broadcast by C.B.C. television. I think here of the broadcast of the program "The Ernie Game" and the other film "Waiting for Caroline", the kind of program that deals with love and sex, couples in bed and so on. Some hon. members would have us believe that there are thousands of people in Canada who are up in arms about this kind of broadcasting. I do not doubt hon. members at all when they say that they have received letters of complaint on this subject. No doubt the headquarters of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation have received similar letters as well. However, I represent a constituency with 120,000 people, an urban constituency largely, and I may have received three letters on this subject.
The answer is not that these people do not watch C.B.C. television because surveys show that about 30 per cent of the people in the lower mainland area of British Columbia regularly watch the local C.B.C. television station. So from a constituency of 120,000 people which is situated in an area of 800,000 people this one member has received two or three letters on this subject. It does not seem to me that there is very much dissatisfaction with the type of broadcasting the people are getting. Therefore I believe that the views expressed by the members to whom I have referred do not represent the views of the majority of the Canadian people.
It seems to me that these members share the point of view of a lot of people who seem to think that our society is going to hell and that our morals are slipping. The people who
5860	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting hold this point of view quite frequently support it by quoting statistics of the number of illegitimate births, the number of divorces and that type of thing in support of their contention that society is going down hill. They seem to yearn for the Victorian age when they think that everything was better. The hon. member for Brandon-Souris referred to it as the good old Victoria days. Many of us think that it was the age of hypocrisy and that the people were not so good. If we accept the point of view of these members that the morals of our society are slipping and that things are not the way they were in the good old days, then let us discuss t.v. programs in that context.
When we talk of t.v. programs that deal with morals or sex, the kind of subject matter about which the hon. members have complained, we are not talking about many hours during a week. We may be talking about the Sunday night public affairs program on occasion, which lasts for one hour. We may be talking about the program "Festival", which is another hour. But we are not talking about very much more than that. The rest of the viewing time is given up to comedy shows, variety shows, public affairs, news, sports. So we are speaking about two or three hours of television a week at the most. I suggest to the committee that if our morals are slipping and the situation is so bad, then we must look somewhere else than to television for the reason. Because two or three hours of television a week, even of the worst sort, cannot be making that much of a contribution to the decline in moral behaviour.
I suggest that we should look at our total environment. We should look at the books that are being sold in the stores every day. I am not talking of the kind of books that only moral deviates would buy; I am talking of books that can be purchased in respectable bookstores, in drugstores and at our leading airports. I refer, for example, to books like "Valley of the Dolls". I asked one book dealer what kind of people bought these books and I found it was not just young kids who may be looking for a thrill. The buyers cut right across the whole spectrum of society. Respectable middle-aged people are buying these books. I suspect that throughout our history people have always been interested in books which have a little pornography in them. These books are purchased by people who are considered to be quite normal in our society. I suggest, there must be some reason why magazines such as Playboy enjoy such wide

DEBATES	January 23, 1968
circulation. It is not only deviates or abnormal people who buy them; in fact they are to be found in the homes of many respectable families.

Somebody says it is in the parliamentary library, Mr. Chairman. I did not know that. I have seen Esquire in the reading room but not Playboy.
Again, Mr. Chairman, looking at the total environment let us look to advertising both in newspapers and magazines and on television which depicts scantily clad ladies advertising various types of underwear. I myself have no objection to this but if our morals are slipping, as people say, then this sort of advertising has something to do with it.
I suggest we should also look to our movies. We must remember here that ideas of censorship have been changing over the years. It used to be the case that in the days of the Hays office married couples in bedroom scenes always had to be shown in separate beds. This has changed; things are changing all the time. People are not shocked by this. There is nothing wrong with it. Why pick on two or three hours of television a week as contributing to the so-called decline in the morals of our society?
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Here, Mr. Chairman, we have an attempt at censorship. Some are saying "Tighten up; don't show that sort of thing." With all due respect to my hon. friend from Red Deer, I suspect he would want nothing more sexy than Anne of Green Gables on television. This amounts to censorship. It does not matter whether we have a board of censors or whether we tell the management of the broadcasting companies to do their own censoring. To be consistent we should have censorship all along the line. We must censor advertising, we must control the sale of books and what goes into books. Advertising can be very suggestive, whether it appears in newspapers, magazines or on television. All communications media would have to be controlled. If this sort of thing were tried in today's 1968 society it would fail utterly. People would not accept it.
I do not accept the view that society is going to hell, as some hon. members seem to think. Rather, I agree with what the hon. member for St. John's West said. Some aspects of life which hon. members do not
January 23, 1968

like to see portrayed are simply more apparent and open than they were before. Hon. members have only to read the biographies of some of the leading lights of the Victorian age to realize that the upper classes and intellectuals were not all that good. They did not practice all the Victorian morals.
We have a more honest and open society today and there is no reason for that not to be reflected on television just as other aspects of our society are reflected there and elsewhere. I want to see a television system which is open and frank in its portrayal of our society. There are laws in this country to deal with anything that goes too far, whether it be in the printed or the visual media. Those laws should be the only restriction.
I make these points particularly for the benefit of the new president and new executive vice president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Perhaps the corporation does need tightening up so far as economy is concerned. I do not know. That is a matter for experts. But I hope that they leave their creative people with a free hand to broadcast. I hope they are free to innovate and experiment. If ever the day comes when members of parliament do not rise to their feet and complain about something the C.B.C. will be a tame organization indeed.
I am really tired of listening to hon. members who act as if they speak for the majority of the Canadian people. I do not think that the majority of the Canadian people object to a few sexy scenes on television. They seem to like those scenes in books and movies, which seems to be a perfectly normal human reaction that has been pretty consistent throughout history.

Mr. Chairman, I was speaking on a point that was raised in the rejection by the Board of Broadcast Governors of C.A.T.V. applications for licences for a number of centres in Canada and the B.B.G.'s concern that they would interfere with the economic viability of local television stations. I wish to pursue that subject further along the line of asking when the cabinet of Canada adopted the attitude that television stations must show a profit each year, even though that means restricting the freedom of access to information and knowledge of the Canadian public.
I made reference a short time ago to the report of Mr. Robert Fowler, which is popularly known as the Fowler report on broadcasting. I was quoting from page 253 of his 27053-370^
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting report in which, though his terms of reference excluded C.A.T.V. operations, he made comments that were not required under his terms of reference. On page 253 he said:
There are, however, many single-channel areas where regulatory policy to nourish or support the licensee has been negated by the sudden intrusion of a number of new signals which dilute the audience and damage commercial support.
The question now arises, why does the Canadian cabinet consider it necessary to provide a financial profit for a television station in the face of the sudden emergence of competition by a C.A.T.V. installation in the area that the local television station is servicing?
I have a brother who was the publisher, for Lord Thomson, of a paper in the Timmins area, the Timmins Press. When he was appointed publisher of that paper by Roy Thomson, as he was then, there was no television station in Timmins. There were applications in hand by the C.B.C. to issue television licences in Timmins. It was well known that television applications had been forwarded to the C.B.C. But did the Canadian cabinet go to the locally established newspaper in Timmins and ask them whether it would be economically viable for them to continue to publish in Timmins and service the general public there if a television station were licensed? Not on your life. The local newspaper in Timmins could sink or swim, according to the financial support it could engender for itself in Timmins, after a television licence was granted.
A television licence was granted to a station in Timmins and the local paper did not object. They were going to live despite the competition, and the television station went on the air. It drew off a tremendous amount of advertising revenue from the local business firms and from national advertisers, but the local Timmins Press continued to publish and continued to show a profit. Why did the cabinet not say to the television applicant, "You cannot operate a station in Timmins because that will adversely affect the economic viability of the presently established mass medium in Timmins?" But no, they licensed the television station.
When a C.A.T.V. operator comes along and wants to operate in an area where a television station has already been established he is told, through the medium of the Board of Broadcast Governors: "That will adversely affect the local television station; you must not go there and adversely affect the local television station. We do not mind how much
January 23, 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting speakers on the matter. In the white paper on broadcasting reference is made on page 7 to the right to freedom of expression, which it says should be unquestioned. I have already emphasized the fact that this begs the whole matter because having the right to freedom of expression where the public does not have the right to receive that expressed opinion is a denial of the right of the individual to receive information from whatever source he so desires.
Then at page 13 of the white paper we read:
Among the matters subject to regulation-will be the inclusion of Canadian channels-
No C.A.T.V. installation in Canada is in the position of not having available all Canadian channels on its dial. When the statement is made that among the matters subject to regulation will be the inclusion of Canadian channels this is a soft way of stating that we are going to do our best to keep American channels off C.A.T.V. installations. I point out that C.A.T.V. is making such rapid strides at the present time that there are now wires available that will carry 30 channels to the individual dial of a C.A.T.V. subscriber. In this way the Canadian government could demand that every television station in Canada be placed on the dial of the local C.A.T.V. operator, even though he cannot pick up all the stations as most of them would be too distant for reception. But the new wires will carry 30 channels now.
There is one operation in South Carolina at the present time with 23 channels available on one wire. So, when the statement is made in the white paper that "among the matters subject to regulation... will be the inclusion of Canadian channels". I would like to add that with these wires now carrying up to a total of 30 channels there is no problem in carrying all the Canadian channels in a specified area. If the viewer wants to look at them he can. If he does not want to look at them then he does not have to look at them.
On the first page of Bill No. C-163 we And it stated that "the right to freedom of expression ... is unquestioned." But the public is denied the right to receive freedom of expression over C.A.T.V. stations. As recorded in Hansard of November 1, 1967, page 3747, the Secretary of State said:
-broadcasters must be allowed the right to freedom of expresion; that is to say, censorship and pre-editing of programs are not only undesirable but impractical.

They certainly are undesirable and in large measure they are impractical, but what is the use of having freedom of expression without censorship if the public is not allowed to look at the programs they want to look at because they are denied a C.A.T.V. franchise in the areas in which they live?
Then we find on page 1348 of the minutes of the committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts for December 1, 1966, that Mr. J. A. Ouimet, president of the C.B.C. told the committee:
Community antenna television (CATV) is to be made part of the broadcasting structure.
When he made that statement on December 1, 1966, it was interesting to many people in the broadcasting and receiving field in this country because no definite statement had been made in that regard prior thereto. I have in my hand a release from the C.B.C. information services, 1500 Bronson avenue, Ottawa, dated January 16, 1967, about six weeks after Mr. Ouimet's statement on community antenna television, and I wish to read it to the committee. It reads:
For Your Information.
The following statement by President Ouimet was released to the Canadian Press in Ottawa; C.B.C. newsrooms; and dailies in Toronto after 7.40 p.m. January 14, 1967:
The C.B.C. is deeply disturbed by the violence of the reaction to its invitation to Mr. Adolph Von Thadden to be interviewed on the program "Sunday." The invitation was based on the rise of Mr. Von Thadden's party in Germany as reported in the news media recently.
Then there is this paragraph:
The greatest safeguard of the democratic tradition is the freedom to express and examine the widest range of ideas and opinions. A prime function and responsibility of the C.B.C. is to provide for the free expression and scrutiny of points of view thus enabling the Canadian people to judge such views for themselves.
Mr. Ouimet never made a more forthright or more honest statement than that contained in that second paragraph in which he said:
The greatest safeguard of the democratic tradition is the freedom to express and examine the widest range of ideas and opinions.
In this broadcasting bill we are told that the freedom of expression is unlimited, but the government does not go along with Mr. Ouimet's statement, namely:
The greatest safeguard of the democratic tradition is the freedom to express and examine the widest range of ideas and opinions. A prime function and responsibility of the C.B.C. is to provide for the free expression and scrutiny of points of view-
January 23, 1968

He did not stop, like this bill does in clause 2, with a mouth-filling statement that freedom of expression is unquestioned and is to be allowed. He went on to say "free expression and scrutiny of points of view." By denying the Canadian public the right to look at programs of their choice over C.A.T.V. installations, which do not fall within the public domain as they do not use radio frequencies which are in the public domain, we are denying the public the right to examine the different points of view and opinion available and to scrutinize points of view, even though we tell the broadcaster he can say what he likes because his freedom of expression is unlimited. But unfortunately the recipient is limited in his choice of scrutiny of programs available on C.A.T.V. installations. In his press release Mr. Ouimet continued:
I must therefore announce the withdrawal of the invitation to come to Canada and telegram to this effect has been sent to him.
This action does not mean that the corporation will abrogate its responsibility in terms of the principle of the right of the Canadian public to information.
I am mighty glad to know that the corporation will not abrogate its responsibility in terms of the principle of the right of the Canadian public to information. But the cabinet is abrogating its responsibility in terms of the principle of the right of the Canadian public to information when, through media such as this proposed council, C.A.T.V. installations will be prohibited from going into certain areas because they will dilute the audiences of the local t.v. stations. The right to information is curtailed when a C.A.T.V. system is placed in the position where it may not be granted a licence.
I have read many references to freedom of expression as though it entirely covered the subject. Free expression is only half of the subject of free speech. The other half is the freedom to hear.
I would like to make a brief reference now to a certain situation which agitates the people in the Toronto-Barrie area. If you look at this bill as amended and reported by the committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts you will find that in clause 19 on page 10 no change whatever has been made in the regulations that make it possible for the cabinet to move the Barrie t.v. station into the Toronto area. Clause 19 is headed "Hearings and Procedure." It states:
A public hearing shall be held by the council (a) In connection with the issue of a broadcasting licence, other than a licence to carry on a temporary network operation-

I am entering this debate as a person who has not had the opportunities that many other hon. members have had for education, cultural development, and so on. I am approaching this question purely as a backwoodsman, you understand, Mr. Chairman.
I referred to the dictionary to ascertain the meaning of the word "should". The two dictionaries which I consulted referred me to the word "shall" and I found in one case a column and in another a column and a half of definitions with respect to its meaning. I have heard this subject discussed on many occasions, namely, the exact meaning of the words "may", "would", "should" and "shall" and after reading the definitions I have come to the conclusion that it is very difficult to say what is the exact distinction between the words "should" and "shall".
I admit frankly that I have not had the opportunities of many distinguished gentlemen in the house, but in my opinion the word "shall" connotes more of a moral imperative than the word "should". On that account I support the hon. member for Lapointe on this occasion, though I differ with him fundamentally in his philosophy in respect of other matters. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the house that Interprovincial Pipe Line Company through its United States subsidiary, Lakehead Pipe Line Company, Inc., has received a presidential permit covering the construction of additional pipe line facilities across the international boundary.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
Although Interprovincial's pipe line system was progressively built to serve the prairies and Ontario, in the course of the years the company has acquired customers in the United States extending from the Saint Paul-Min-neapolis area to Buffalo, N.Y. Increasing demand in all these markets has required a substantial increase of Interprovincial's facilities. In order to meet anticipated demand in Ontario and elsewhere in 1968 and for subsequent years and to restore the reserve
5870	COMMONS
Pipe Line Across International Boundary capacity it normally carries for national and international purposes, the company has to undertake further expansion immediately.
In view of this further expansion Interprovincial considers it desirable to loop its facilities east of Superior, Wisconsin, south of its existing line, before re-entering Canada. The first step contemplated by Interprovincial is the construction of a 34-inch line from Superior to the Chicago area, to be completed some time in 1968.
In the near future, probably in 1969, Interprovincial will construct a 30-inch connecting line from that area to Port Huron to complete the loop. The timing of such further construction would depend on a number of matters, including the terms and conditions under which the Tecumseh and Buckeye systems are available to Interprovincial in the meantime, and the rate of growth in demand in the areas served by Interprovincial. I would expect that Interprovincial will proceed immediately to the construction of its new facilities.
The house should also be aware that the Aurora-Glacier pipe line system, which transports oil from Alberta into Montana, is currently undergoing expansion. This expansion is associated with a further presidential permit, which has been issued.
These programs of expansion of facilities were included in recent discussions on oil with the United States authorities which, as the house knows, take place periodically. These discussions and exchanges are used to explore the potential levels of our exports as well as the relationships of our two countries on oil matters generally. From these conversations come the mutual confidence which facilitates the efforts of our industry to increase exports while avoiding disruption of United States markets. The recent discussions have been no exception to this rule. An important feature contributing to the framework of agreement which came out of our meetings was the clarification that Interprovincial has planned its expansion with a view to the future as well as to immediate markets. A similar element of pre-investment is also present in the expansion program of the Aurora-Glacier system.
I am sure the house would wish to commend the industry and the pipe line companies for their initiative regarding the projects to which I have referred. They will have the effect of placing our industry in a sound position to meet the future requirements in Ontario and United States markets in an efficient

and economic manner. These projects are also a manifestation of the ability of government departments and agencies on both sides of the border to resolve matters of common interest in an atmosphere of good will.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian private company, Interprovincial Pipe Line, should be congratulated for being able to get into the Chicago market. In the first stage this will increase our exports into the market by approximately 50,000 barrels a day and it will go some way toward balancing the deficit which exists between our imports and exports, with resulting benefits to Canada's balance of payments. While welcoming this announcement there is one point I have to emphasize, namely, the fact that we still lack from the government a statement on a national oil policy. In the original oil policy statement of 1961 we declared unilaterally as the Canadian government that exports from Canada should approximate imports into the Montreal and maritime markets. That was the first principle in the national oil policy. The second principle was that our producers should be allowed to produce at their maximum rate of efficiency which should roughly equal that of the United States independent producers. The statement of 1961 succeeded in increasing our exports to a point where they almost balanced our imports.
Since 1963 there has been no statement from the government regarding the objectives which private enterprise should meet in implementing this oil policy. It must be admitted that the pressure on the United States government by independent companies in the United States to restrict their country's market has made it difficult for us to deal with that government. The Israeli-Arab war of last year broke the dike, and now I think the United States government recognizes the inherent dangers. The decisions that have been made in the last year with regard to our resources have enhanced Canada's economic position immensely.
The economics of today's announcement are sound. As Alaska oil moved into the west coast of the United States it made it more difficult for our western Canadian producers to enter the northwestern American market. So it is only natural for us to allow Alaska oil to move into the west and to move our oil into the mid-west regions of the United States. The pipe line extension from Superior to Chicago will allow us first entry into that
January 23, 1968

market through the pipe line, and the extension from Port Huron to Sarnia will assure people in Ontario that their immediate needs in the next few years will be met by this increased capacity.
From the viewpoint of a Canadian nationalist I believe that this announcement is good for Canada. As the minister said, it is also good for the United States. I believe that Canadians will have to live with the fact that if we are to get the maximum and best use of our resources we must think and talk in terms of mutual advantage to both countries. The primary rule should be that prices should be as low as possible for the consumers in all parts of North America and therefore products should move into the best markets. The midwest market is a good market for western oil.
The second rule which should be followed is that producers should be allowed to obtain the best price they can realize for their fuel in the competitive markets. The movement into this field has brought new opportunities in the last two years for Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan to find markets in a natural and economic way. This move by Interprovincial Pipe Line is not only sound economically but also fits into what I conceive to be the basis of a national oil policy which the government should announce. I hope the government will take cognizance of the advice that we have been trying to give them for the last four or five years, namely, that in the interest of all Canadians and of the whole North American continent the government should periodically state its objectives in the national oil policy, keeping in mind the criteria I have mentioned.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that private enterprise shows beyond doubt that it is anxious to serve the interests of the nation even though my hon. friend for York South (Mr. Lewis) says that the companies will make profits. I believe that they will show profits and will develop our resources more profitably than any government could. In fact, their operations will be profitable, whereas a government body would show a deficit. This is shown everywhere, even in Saskatchewan where a socialist government, at one time, led the province without achieving a balanced budget.
So, I think we should congratulate private enterprise for showing initiative and developing natural resources in order to serve the best interests of the country, because it will use Canadian manpower, Canadian material, while encouraging the producers of our country.

That is why I feel that instead of minimizing and crushing private enterprise because it is making profits, a responsible government should rather help private enterprise to develop our natural resources, so that they will serve first the Canadian people, while the surplus can be exported abroad.

At the end of the hour I had been referring to the international ownership of this company and the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, by way of clarification, said something. I did not think he should have made his remarks in the way he made them because I did not want even the briefest remark of the hon. member to close the debate. I wanted an opportunity to say something more.
I wish to read what the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace said because, should he ever have the opportunity to close the debate on second reading, he may wish to elaborate on what he said. He said, as reported on page 3814 of Hansard for November 2, 1967:
For the information of the hon. member this company is a Canadian company, originally incorporated in Manitoba in 1906, and subsequently incorporated under chapter 70 of the statutes of 1910. The original company, Eagle Star, was a British company.
My interpretation of those remarks may be wrong but I took them to mean that the British Northwestern Insurance Company, to which the hon. gentleman is referred, is a Canadian company. Later the hon. gentleman referred to Eagle Star and he said that the parent company was British.
I may have misunderstood the hon. member because I did not appreciate that British Northwestern Insurance Company was a Canadian company in the sense that it is owned and controlled in Canada by Canadians. The contrary was my understanding. I
Private Bills
wish now to quote an extract from the proceedings before the banking and commerce committee of the Senate on June 28, 1967. The committee was considering this bill. I shall quote from page 29 of the proceedings where I find the remarks of Mr. Humphrys, the superintendent of insurance, which, incidentally, were not challenged in any way by anyone who attended that hearing.
In passing I might add that one other person spoke before the committee, a Mr. James Hugessen who is listed as a parliamentary agent. The chairman asked him if he had anything to add, to which Mr. Hugessen said, "No, Mr. Chairman, I have nothing to add." That was the extent of his evidence.
Mr. Humphrys, whose remarks were not challenged in any way, said:
The British Northwestern Insurance Company is a federal company, having been federally incorporated in 1917, but it started earlier as a provincial company. It is owned by the Eagle Star Insurance Company, a prominent British company with worldwide interests and a very large volume of business.
I understood that only two companies were involved in this bill, the British Northwestern Insurance Company and the Eagle Star Insurance Company. One of the purposes of the bill is to change the name of British Northwestern Insurance Company to Eagle Star Insurance Company of Canada. That name would closely approximate the name of the British parent company and would bring with it all the benefits of having a similar name.
The hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace said, "this company is a Canadian company." That is without meaning. The company may have been incorporated under federal law or under the statutes of a province, but since, according to the evidence of Mr. Humphrys, it is controlled in the United Kingdom it is not a Canadian company.
When the hon. member interjected the hour had almost expired and I did not have the opportunity to pursue his remarks. At the time his comments seemed a little odd and on reading them later they still seemed odd. On November 2 I said that if the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace wanted to interrupt me by using the procedure of asking a question I would be glad to accommodate him. But the time expired and the opportunity did not arise. It has arisen now. In any event, I hope the hon. member will wait until he has the opportunity to close the debate before taking advantage of any opportunity that may arise for him to speak.

The approach to this company ought to be the approach adopted with respect to other companies that are foreign owned and controlled and which seek to do something in this country through bills that come before this house. It is well known that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has a particular view on the question of foreign ownership. He has enunciated it in the past. He was speaking as Prime Minister and not as a private individual and his remarks carried the force of the government itself. He said that the Canadian government is partial to the promotion of Canadian ownership of our resources and wealth.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
I believe that as long as the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) remains in office this will be the view taken by the government. But this stand may change early in April, on the 10th or the 11th, or some such date, and it may be that tthe new prime minister will not share this opinion. Incidentally, the new prime minister may not even be able to sit in the House of Commons for some time after that date. He may decide that the sources from which he derived the support which enabled him to assume office were such that he ought to take a more tolerant view regarding this question of the control of insurance and other companies. However, for the time being we must abide by the attitude which the present Prime Minister takes toward this question of foreign ownership, an approach which the hon. gentleman who used to be minister of finance-I do not recall his present office-also used to adopt.
Some years ago this parliament enacted as law certain alterations to the legislation governing insurance companies, requiring that some of these companies, depending upon the date of their formation, must be Canadian owned rather than foreign owned or foreign dominated. Thus the Canadian parliament itself has taken a stand on this question of Canadian ownership.
In my opinion, this reflects the feelings of Canadians themselves. I should like to point out that there is a mechanism by means of which the British Northwestern Insurance Company could bring itself within the purview of public law and establish itself as a Canadian company in a true sense. This mechanism was used voluntarily by the United Investment Life Assurance Company which earlier had a bill before this house and which is currently before the Senate. The

company came to parliament and said voluntarily that it desired to become a full Canadian corporate citizen, even though the original bill for which it had petitioned contained no such provision. That company, therefore, proposed in a memorandum to the committee which considered the legislation that within two years of the commencement of business it would make a public offering to Canadian residents of a sufficient number of shares to bring its share ownership to below 75 per cent. I relate this, though it applies to an entirely different bill, merely because the relevant wording could be extracted and incorporated in the bill now before us by a simple process of substitution.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think I should proceed any further until there is a quorum in the house.

speechtext: Despite the public position of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) with regard to the question of the ownership of business and natural resources in Canada, it does seem to me that Canadians continue to indulge a predilection for shipping out not only our resources but our money in the delusion that we shall thereby continue in a state of prosperity and economic well-being.

It has been drawn to my attention informally that the attendance is somewhat below that called for by the rules. I am not raising this as a point of order but merely by way of comment, because I think the bill before us is an indication of the Canadian predilection to which I have referred.
This measure appears to have a double purpose. According to the explanatory notes, one of them is to change the name of the company and the other is to expand the capital stock of the company. I have decided to address my remarks largely to the second purpose, the proposal to expand the capital stock.
This is a proposal brought before us by what is, as my hon. friend has pointed out, a foreign company despite the fact that it is legally incorporated as a Canadian firm. In these circumstances I suggest it is a matter worthy of careful consideration by hon. members before they decide whether or not the bill should be approved. The proposal here is
January 23, 1968

to raise the number of shares from 50,000 to
125,000,	each having a par value of $40. This represents a substantial expansion. What does it mean in practical terms?
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
It means that any of the surplus which may come into the till as the result of these operations, presumably expanded operations because of the proposal to enlarge the scope of the company and its capital stock, will represent an additional amount of the savings of the Canadian people to be siphoned abroad. From time to time, I and some of my colleagues have attempted to argue in connection with certain other bills that to assent to such a proposition is clearly to aggravate what is already an unfortunate situation so far as the Canadian economy and people are concerned. We have said that far from approving any expansion of private insurance companies in this country, parliament should be taking a stand to call a halt to that expansion. Increasingly, the kind of operations they conduct are an unnecessary and wasteful appendage to the economy of the country.
We have had debates in this house about the expansion of public pension plans. The Canada Pension Plan is a good case in point. During those debates some of us became increasingly aware of the source from which the major opposition to any such plan was stemming. Among other sources, it was coming from the private insurance interests in Canada. On the one hand we have parliament, rather painfully and slowly, struggling to implement measures that will serve the common good of all the Canadian people, and on the other we are being asked to approve and pass bills of this nature which strengthen the hand of the very economic and financial interests that have been seeking to slow down and prevent the enactment of laws to provide adequate public insurance programs.
If I understand correctly the evidence given before the Senate banking and commerce committee, this company operates largely in the field of automobile insurance. It is not in the life insurance business. We do not have across this land any adequate system of public coverage for the hazards of automobile operation, hazards both to the owners and to pedestrians. I believe this is the direction in which we should be moving rather than lending our approval to giving added power and strength to private automobile insurance interests which, in my view, have been conducting a very expensive and
Private Bills
wasteful operation in so far as providing protection is concerned.
I find it astonishing that members who support the government, and after all this is the government that sponsored the Canada Pension Plan measure, can reconcile their positions in acting as sponsors of bills of this nature with their support of measures such as the Canada Pension Plan. These measures have the support of other members of the house but they like to laud them as accomplishments of the party to which they belong. It is time we made up our minds about which direction we are going to move, whether we are to continue the aimless expansion and multiplication of these private insurance companies, placing increased economic power in their hands with which to further their industry, politically and otherwise, or whether we are going to put a halt to that trend. One of the ways in which we can put a halt to that trend is to refuse to pass bills allowing these companies to expand and increase their powers.
This becomes all the more pointed when we realize that we are placing this power in the hands of financial interests that lie beyond the borders of our country.

I am not sure I am in a position to answer completely the hon. member's question. He may have information concerning this proposal which I do not have. In his introductory remarks he did not cover the question which he has asked me, and I have not found an answer to it in the evidence given to the banking and commerce committee of the Senate. In fact, my reading of the brief bit of evidence given to that committee indicates that this company, leaving aside the question of the juggling of various corporations, will remain a company owned and controlled by a large British insurance firm or complex of firms.
I cannot see that the point the hon. member has raised in any way alters the validity of

January 23, 1988
