the argument that I have been making. I am not quite certain whether the hon. member is suggesting that this increased capitalization is simply to enable one company to take over the stock of others. If that is the point he is driving at, it is not made clear in the evidence given to the Senate committee. The explanatory notes say that one of the purposes of the bill is to change the capital stock from 50,000 shares, with a total value of $2 million, to 125,000 shares with a total value of $5 million. That is a very substantial expansion of the capital stock of the company, two and a half times an increase in valuation and number of shares. In any event, whether or not that is the case the basic argument I am making still stands.
In my view it is not in the public interest to pass measures to enable private insurance companies to expand and multiply the fields of their operation, as we have been asked to do by this and a veritable barrage of other bills in recent months and years.
I am trying to say something which I have not said before. The facts of the matter are that within the tussle for the Canadian savings dollar it is becoming increasingly evident that there is a real conflict between what is in the public interest and what is in the interest of a few private and special financial corporations, corporations increasingly owned and controlled outside of our borders. The latter is an undesirable trend, and this parliament should say so in no uncertain terms.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
We must recognize that in a sense this is a political battle which has never clearly emerged on the floor of this chamber. Nevertheless, one has only to read the type of briefs and documents which reach our offices in periods when we have measures before us like the Canada Pension Plan to realize where much of the strength of the opposition to the idea of the expansion of public insurance is, and where the real opposition is to the channelling of the savings of the Canadian people into socially desirable programs. We have had statements made on motions by the Minister of Finance concerning the problem of protecting the Canadian dollar. Yet, so often in this hour we are asked to approve measures which in the long run will simply compound the problems which any minister of finance in this country will have to face in the future.
We say it is important that this measure not be slipped through in this hour of our proceedings because it would have the effect of negating some of the efforts which may

from time to time be made as a matter of public policy to preserve and strengthen the financial position of the country. We believe that the one cannot be separated from the other. Even though these bills are brought in under the guise of private bills during the period which is referred to as private mem bers' hour, it is my contention that basically we are here to enhance and protect the interests of the ordinary people of Canada. This is the point of view to which we should address ourselves when proposals of this kind come forward. I do not believe this should be regarded as a place to which any private interest can come and expect to get placid and tacit consent by members of parliament to proposals which would enhance their interests at the expense of the ordinary citizens ot Canada.
These private bills, as I have seen them g< through this house from session to session have had a lasting effect upon the real nature of the economy of this country. I do not believe the implications which are inherent in these proposals should be ignored by this house to the extent they often are. This attitude is often indicated by the kind of attendance we have in the house when these matters are considered. I believe we should serve notice-at least I am prepared to do so-that there are some members in this parliament who are not prepared to bow down three times whenever an insurance company decides it wishes to do something in this country. We should make it clear we do not intend to continue to silently accept their sabotage, which is going on behind the scenes, of measures which will really enhance the position of the Canadian people. These are the types of road blocks which stand in the way of real social advances, and which these people manage to establish through their propaganda as well as in other ways.
This is something which disturbs me most deeply. I know we could have had a Canada pension plan which would have been much more adequate than the one now on the statute books had these companies not been so successful in pulling the strings behind the scenes to prevent this kind of a plan. Therefore, while some people allege privately if not on the floor of the house that this is an obstructive exercise, I should like to tell you that so far as I am concerned this is a constructive exercise. It is an effort to persuade this parliament that it is about time we took notice of what is being slipped through during these private members' hours. It is about time we started putting the interests of our
January 23, 1968	COMMONS
people before the private interests of foreign insurance companies.
I believe this bill, with its proposed terms, is a very good example of how we can continue this process that is working against the interests of our constituents. We should be prepared to take a stand and say that it will go on no longer. I am not suggesting that this company or any one of these companies should be expropriated or put out of business.
I am saying, however, that this kind of wasteful approach to the whole field of insurance should be stopped where it is, and that from now on we should agree that public insurance can be provided much more economically and much more effectively than insurance has been provided in the past by virtue of the laws enabling these companies to operate and to expand.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock I had made some reference to the fact that in this new broadcasting bill No. C-163 the power still resides with the cabinet to override the decisions of the proposed new council, if as and when it may desire. I made particular reference to the situation existing in the Toronto-Barrie area where a tremendous uproar developed some time ago when it was ascertained by the residents of Toronto that it would be possible for one member of the cabinet only, by putting his signature on a single piece of paper, to move the Barrie station in such a direction and to such an extent that it would interfere with reception in Toronto of several very popular television stations in the Toronto area. I pointed out that there has been no change made in this regard.
Let me direct your attention to the proposal in this bill which states that the governor in council may override any decision of the council as long as it is done within 60 days and as long as the matter has been referred again to the council which has made a second report to the cabinet. However, if that council should have occasion to make a decision the cabinet does not like, arrangements can be
5878	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting made to change the personnel on the council. There are many of us in this house old enough to remember the treatment by Lloyd George of the British House of Lords. When it came time to put a certain measure through the House of Lords he simply created lords right and left in order to obtain a majority in support of his own opinion.
We had a recent appointment to the B.B.G. which was very important, because after he took his seat the motion he was looking after carried by a majority of one. According to the best information available no one has denied the source of that majority, even though the motion was passed the same day as that great Liberal took his seat for the first time.
This situation has to be watched carefully. I believe there should be a change in this proposed bill regarding television and radio because the Canadian public is not satisfied with the situation as it is today. A license can be granted to a t.v. station operator to set up business in a certain town. An amendment to that license can be made by the council if it is desired. Why can a license not be granted for a specific point and for that point only? I have been active for many years in the newspaper business. The newspapers I was connected with were always associated with the Canadian Press. The Canadian Press is a cooperative news gathering organization, but I can assure you that when the Canadian Press granted membership to a new applicant at some place where a new daily paper was to be established that did not give the new member the opportunity to move to any other city in Canada he thought would offer him a better financial return than the place from which he made his application. If a t.v. station operator has applied for a license to go into a certain centre and a licence is granted, there should not be any clause which would make it possible for that operator to move that t.v. station elsewhere, if, as and when he decided to do so. This should not be possible as the result only of obtaining the assent of the cabinet or the proposed new council for radio and television. Such a decision can be made at a meeting in secret. As I indicated to you before six o'clock, meetings do not have to be held in public if the executive committee decides there is no necessity.
Before moving on to the proposed method of financing the C.B.C. on the basis of five year grabs, I should like to refer to a portion of the white paper in relation to multiple

DEBATES	January 23, 1968
ownership of mass media in any one community. I read to you from page ten of the 1966 white paper on broadcasting. On page 12 we have a section headed "Ownership of Canadian facilities". It reads in part:
Within Canada, ownership or control of one medium of communication by another is equally a matter of concern if it tends to develop into a monopoly. There is a growing number of cases where either ownership or control extends to both the local newspapers and the local radio or television facilities. The Board of Broadcast Governors will be required to investigate and report on public complaints or representations about situations of this kind.
Let me point out that there is one city in this Dominion of Canada where the newspaper and the television station are owned by one organization. This is a monopoly situation if there ever was one. I am not going to attack that monopoly situation on the ground that it is inimical to the public interest. However, when people have applied for a C.A.T.V. licence to enter the area served by the monopoly, the newspaper and television station owner-and incidentally the radio station owner as well-they have been told that this would inhibit the establishment of a second television facility in that area. Here is a prima facie case where businessmen have offered competition to a monopoly situation involving the local newspaper, radio and television stations yet the Board of Broadcast Governors say no, you cannot go in there and offer competitive service because this would inhibit the possibility of an alternative t.v. station being erected there.
The white paper was prepared by the cabinet, make no mistake about that. The white paper, says the governor will look into monopoly situations. They should, particularly in relation to a C.A.T.V. application for a license to open a station to break a monopoly situation. Yet any one who makes such an application is informed that he can not do that; he simply can not do that.

They are fine sounding words in the white paper, but I say that actions speak louder than words. The action in refusing a C.A.T.V. applicant permission to enter a monopoly area indicates more forcibly what the cabinet desires to do than any words that may be found in the white paper or in any broadcasting committee report, I can assure you.
Before leaving the subject of C.A.T.V for a moment I should like to refer to the remarks
January 23, 1968

of the hon. Secretary of State on November 1, 1967, to be found on page 3749 of Hansard:
Provision is made for the exemption of certain classes of community antenna from the licensing requirements, for example, the roof-top antenna on an apartment block-
I ask you, if the roof-top antenna on an apartment block, which is nothing more or less than a community antenna system, is not going to require a licence why do they have to have licences for other forms of community antenna systems? As most of you are aware, I represent a Toronto riding. I have been a resident of Toronto for over 50 years. I think it is absolutely amazing that the cabinet will make the statement, through the Secretary of State, that no licence will be required for a roof-top antenna on an apartment block, but other forms of C.A.T.V. operations must have a licence.
I point out, too, that no licence is required for a roof-top antenna to serve a hotel the size of the Royal York hotel in Toronto, which has a community antenna pure and simple. But if there is a real estate subdivision anywhere in Canada that wishes to put in a community antenna in order to bring in the largest possible number of stations to the people living in the real estate subdivision, they will have to apply to this new radio television council for a licence. How ridiculous can you be? You do not need a licence to have a roof-top antenna on a 24-floor apartment block such as stands across the Humber river from my home in the riding of York-Humber. You do not need a licence for a community antenna to service the Royal York hotel, the King Edward hotel or the Westbury hotel. But if the owners of a real estate subdivision desire to put up a community antenna and bury the wires underneath the ground so that every house will not have an antenna above it picking up the individual family reception, they have to apply for a licence, which may be refused by the Board of Broadcast Governors or this proposed new council.
It cannot be right that hotels and apartment blocks do not need a licence for their community antenna systems, whereas real estate subdividers will have to apply for a licence in order to service the homes in the subdivision. If a town wants C.A.T.V., the operator there must apply for a licence. I guess the best way to get a C.A.T.V. licence in Napanee, Prescott and Gananoque would be to erect a hotel consisting of a couple of floors and put in a community antenna system.
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
I was quite interested when a member of the house last night came to me and talked about C.A.T.V. I said I had never subscribed to it until about two weeks ago. The reason I now subscribe to the C.A.T.V. system is this: I did not really need it, because I was getting a clear enough picture on black and white television, but when I secured a coloured television set-by the way, my wife and I paid for it ourselves; the C.B.C. did not pay for it-I decided to have C.A.T.V. installation in order to get a clearer picture on the coloured television set.
The member of the House of Commons who spoke to me last night said that he does not believe the freedom of the individual is being interfered with by the necessity of securing a licence for C.A.T.V. He expressed resentment to me because I get the C.A.T.V. service from the antenna on top of the Old Mill Towers. He said it is okay for the Old Mill Towers, a 24-floor apartment house, to pick the signals out of the air and transmit them to the apartment dwellers on the 24 floors, but he expressed resentment at the fact that man has a licence to service an area of about a square mile around the Old Mill Towers. He expressed resentment at private homes within a mile of Old Mill Towers receiving C.A.T.V., although it was all right to give it to the apartment dwellers. It was a member of the House of Commons who expressed that resentment last night, much to my surprise.
While we are speaking about the heart of the matter, which is clause 2 of this Bill No. C-163, I want to make some references to the proposed method of financing this octopus which has the country in its grip. In the relevant clauses of the proposed legislation it is stated definitely as follows:
Upon the coming into force of this act and every fifth year thereafter, the corporation shall submit to the minister for submission to the governor in council a five-year capital program proposed by the corporation together with a forecast of the effect of the program on the corporation's operating requirements.
No one can quarrel with the desire to have a five year capital expenditure program submitted by the corporation to the cabinet, because you cannot make large capital expenditures within a 12 month period; capital expenditures, generally speaking, are for long range programs. But I cannot for one single moment support subclause 2 of the financing operation of the corporation which suggests to this parliament that:
Upon the coming into force of this act and every fifth year thereafter, the corporation shall submit
January 23, 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting to the minister an operating budget for the next ensuing five financial years of the corporation for approval by the governor in council on the recommendation of the minister and the treasury board, and the minister shall lay before parliament each such operating budget of the corporation as approved by the governor in council within 15 days after the approval thereof or, if parliament is not then sitting, on any of the first 15 days next thereafter that parliament is sitting.
This simply means that the C.B.C. is to be given their money in five year grabs. Mr. Chairman and members of the Canadian House of Commons, this to me is an absolute denial of democracy. It is a denial of democracy because the control of public expenditure and taxation is at the heart of the parliamentary system and its origins are deeply rooted in history. The evolution of the British constitution was largely influenced by the fundamental principle that no taxes should be levied and no public revenues disbursed without the prior approval of the representatives of the citizens and taxpayers in parliament assembled. This principle is so fundamental that it is impossible to assign a date to its origin.
I would point out that the practice of holding regular sessions of parliament may be said to date effectively from the passage of the Bill of Rights in 1689. The principle of granting annual appropriations can be traced back in more rudimentary form to the parliaments of the Stuart kings. Prior to 1641 Charles I governed for 11 years without summoning a parliament. It was to resist these illegal exactions that the House of Commons, whenever there was a parliament in existence, would insist on an annual review of certain grants. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, what is the reason for calling parliament back once a year if we are going to give this crown corporation their money in five year grabs?
The explanation was given to us in the committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts that the C.B.C. wanted to get their money in five-year grabs so they would not have to come to parliament and ask for the money every 12 months; it was said this would interfere with the even tenor of their acts. A further study of the matter disclosed the point that in 1957, under the St. Laurent administration, there was established by the parliament of Canada the Canada Council. Before the creation of the Canada Council, you may remember, certain great windfalls came to the dominion in the form of succession duties on two vast Canadian estates which were assigned to the Canada Council

over a ten year period. I have read the discussion and observed the fact that parliament was being circumvented by this ten-year plan for the Canada Council. I refer to the discussion that took place in 1957.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I am glad to see that the hon. member for Cariboo is in the house tonight because I should like to pay tribute to him for the stand he took in February of 1957, almost 11 years ago, against money being voted by parliament on a ten year basis. He mentioned the fact that money should not be voted for a longer term than one year and that each year parliament should impose the necessary taxes and allocate funds to the departments requiring finance. I should like to refer in more detail to the statements of the hon. member for Cariboo. They make very interesting reading at this time when there is an effort afoot to allocate money to the C.B.C. in five year grants. I tell you, gentlemen, if the C.B.C. can foretell what will happen in five years' time, they should be running the country. Let me point out that this past Sunday the Prime Minister of Canada himself, speaking in Winnipeg, pointed out that there are unhappy signs of difficulties ahead. He said that prices and the danger of inflation are a major problem and that the government has begun to tackle it. The Globe and Mail of January 22 contained the following report:
Canada's dollar remains strong, although there are unhappy signs of a weakening in international economic co-operation, Prime Minister Lester Pearson told western Liberals here yesterday.
Then we have the comments of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in his year end review of Canada's economy in 1967 and outlook for 1968. The minister, who is a master at his job, said the following:
In Canada, economic activity has continued to expand, but at a reduced pace.... But more than half of this increase reflects higher prices.
Then, he pointed out that:
Above average wheat crops, particularly in the main importing countries, have brought about a pronounced softening in the world wheat market in the latter part of 1967.
The C.B.C. of course will be able to foretell whether or not there will be above average wheat crops in other parts of the world thus affecting Canadian wheat sales from year to year, and therefore we should give them their money in five year grants.

Then, the Minister of Trade and Commerce went on to say:
There are, however, other, less salutary, developments in the economy which, unless checked, could reverse this favourable trend in our payments position and undermine the very basis of our current prosperity.
The minister has his feet on the ground. He knows no man can look into the future five years ahead. It is a fortunate man who can look 12 months ahead. He went on to say:
Nor can the momentum toward freer world trade be allowed to subside.
He issued his statement in December and already in January we are concerned about the protective policies which are developing in various nations of the world. We cannot foretell which country will raise barriers against us at any one time, but the C.B.C. management maintain they can foretell five years ahead what will happen, despite rising costs, despite inflation, and despite above average wheat crops in other parts of the world. The C.B.C. knows what will happen. They can tell us five years in advance what they will want, and we are supposed to pay them the money without any discussion during the five year period.
The following is a quotation by the hon. member for Cariboo of what Hon. Louis St. Laurent said on the establishment of the Canada Council:
It was for the purpose of creating this body in such a way that it would not be subject to frequent pressures in the allocation of the funds which would be placed at its disposal.
This simply means that Mr. St. Laurent did not want the Canada Council coming to parliament once every 12 months to ask for additional funds. He referred to it as being "subject to frequent pressures in the allocation of funds". This is a nice way of speaking of annual grants by the parliament of Canada to which men and women are elected to look after the best interests of the taxpayers. As the hon. member for Cariboo said in February of 1957:
-I think it is a reflection on any government, ... to make the suggestion he did, namely that someone who is going to follow is not going to be as true to his country as the Prime Minister himself is.
If the C.B.C. cannot trust the parliaments which will be elected in the future to do the proper thing year by year, then we need somebody in the C.B.C. with a little trust and faith in the elected members of this house.
To show hon. members how impossible it is even for the C.B.C. to forecast the future I

He spoke at that time about the changes that had taken place since June when he brought in the first budget. He referred to the financial changes which had taken place in the previous five months. On November 30, the Minister of Finance said the following:
The fiscal restraints that are essential now may limit somewhat the increase in our production next year but such a limitation now is far better than a serious recession later... This is a case where the proverbial ounce of prevention now is far preferable to a pound of cure later.
He then spoke of:
-the unacceptably high rate at which prices and costs are increasing, including wage settlements.
He referred to cost increases and said:
-in the expectation that their money over the years will maintain its real value.

Mr. Chairman, I was rather hesitant at rising at this stage of the proceedings because I question the value of suggestions that are put forward at this stage. However, some of the suggestions I wish to make in my presentation may be of such a nature that something can be done to implement them. I mention this because I wonder whether there can be many major changes in the drafting of this bill before it finally passes parliament, if it does.
I venture to suggest to the minister at this point that in the few months remaining until


the new leader of the government is appointed she temper her remarks so that the new management of the C.B.C. might be given the opportunity to prove its value, if such is the case.
One suggestion I should like to leave at this point of the proceedings and which applies to broadcasting generally concerns the programming of the C.B.C. about which there has been wide criticism from the public at large. People feel that in many cases the C.B.C. programming is demoralizing, deceitful and degrading. This is not criticism that is levelled by church groups or organizations which seek to provide us with some sort of standard of values in this country; this is criticism that has come from parents as well as from young people.
We have from time to time passed legislation relating to pornography, and this subject is also occasionally touched on by the C.B.C. in its television broadcasting. If magazines or books are published in contravention of such legislation, then they should be withdrawn or action taken.
Some producers produce programs with only one idea in mind, namely their self-promotion. In such cases, I think it would be in the public interest to stipulate in their contracts that if after consultation with the management and board of directors of the C.B.C. they are of the opinion that certain programs of this type were detrimental to the moral health of the country, the contracts of these producers could be terminated. A provision could be written into the contract to safeguard the producer's interest, but I think that some action along this line is necessary. I do not think that the public in general should be subjected to this type of program whether they want it or not. Although this criticism is mainly directed at the C.B.C., it could also apply to private broadcasters. That is all I have to say on that point. I do not want to spend more time than is necessary briefly to state the case.
I am also opposed to another provision in the bill, which incidentally has been embodied in other legislation. I am referring to the appointment of the president, which is now a thing of the past. I do not think that such appointments should be made for a period longer than four years. If at the end of the four year period the incumbent has been satisfactory he could be reappointed. In the case of a man who has proved his value I do not think there would be any danger of the government suddenly dismissing him and trying to find somebody to take his place.
January 23, 1S68

In my opinion this would provide some recourse to the government if the management of the C.B.C. were unable to apply themselves to the promotion of the type of programming that was considered desirable.
I would join other speakers in voicing my objection to the five year period for capital programming. I cannot imagine anything more undesirable than perpetuating the type of financing of the C.B.C. that has been the case heretofore and which has been progressively increasing in amount year by year.
In this connection, one has only to look back to previous broadcasting reports and to the report of the Gordon commission to find how sadly underestimated were the financial requirements of broadcasting, and this following upon what I believe was a very care-full study of broadcasting needs. I do not think that the government should be obligated to carry on mistakes in this area which may have been made by its predecessor or by a former leader of the party.
The government is presently attempting to impose an austerity program on the country. This it cannot do if it continues to hand over sizeable amounts to the C.B.C. which are in the interest neither of the public nor the government. I suggest that the financial provisions in the bill should be re-examined. Parliament has never turned down any budgetary plans that were reasonable. However, I do not believe that the public will tolerate the present situation, and I do not think we would be doing our duty if we were not to record our opposition to this particular type of financing.
With regard to capital expenditure, it is regrettable that many fringe areas in the country at the present time are not receiving service and are sadly neglected. I remember asking a question on this on March 9, 1966, and I was told that at that time the total number of people without television in Newfoundland was 83,600; in Prince Edward Island 10,300; in Nova Scotia 8,600; in New Brunswick 11,100; in Quebec 82,300; in Ontario 85,000; in Manitoba 71,300; in my own province of Saskatchewan 169,300; in Alberta
88,000,	and in British Columbia 111,800. There are many areas of the country which are well served with facilities. I know the demand is great, but we should not ignore these people entirely.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
One need only look at the expenditures which have been made on fringe areas to
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting realize what has happened. The information I am about to give to the committee was supplied to me by the C.B.C. At the end of March, $1,700,000 had been spent specifically for the extension of coverage into those areas which might be considered fringe areas. In 1964, $733,000 was spent; in 1965, $1,400,000 was spent; in 1966, $2,700,000, was spent and in 1967, $2,200,000 was spent. As against that, in 1967 alone $10 million was spent for colour television facilities. I understand that that was a special expenditure. Nevertheless, the question is often asked why, after a five year period, only approximately $8 million has been spent in developing coverage for fringe areas, as against the $10 million which was spent for colour television facilities in one year. Such expenditure does not constitute a proper management of funds and shows a complete disregard for those in the fringe areas.
In future, I submit, between 15 to 20 per cent of capital expenditures should be earmarked specifically for our fringe areas. In this way our entire population will come to understand what national unity is. The people in some areas of Canada have grown up with television, but in other areas they have not. Sometimes the television that has been provided has been difficult to view. That this situation is allowed to exist some of our people think is inequitable, it should be corrected.
The question of satellite broadcasting has not even been touched in this bill. I cannot understand why such a supposedly far reaching bill should ignore the question of satellite broadcasting. I submit that under the broadcasting bill we should set up an agency which should look into the entire question of satellite broadcasting and co-ordinate all the preliminary work that may be necessary to bring about such a far reaching innovation as broadcasting via satellite.
We know what is going on between Quebec and France. Satellite television is not something that is in somebody's imagination, something that we shall not see for the next 20 years. Satellite television is a present day reality and this bill ought to make provision for this country to control the space above it from which a satellite might beam broadcasts. We might launch a satellite in orbit. In any event, I think we should try to protect ourselves, because other countries are looking at space.
Do we want satellite transmissions to be controlled by private or public agencies? That
January 23, 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting is a question we must ask ourselves and that is the question which this bill should clarify. But this bill does nothing like that. At present the initiative in this field comes from private industry. The question that Canadians generally may ask themselves is: is it necessary to have a Canadian Broadcasting Corporation at all?

speechtext: Yes.

speechtext:
If the answer is yes, as an hon. member suggests, I submit that it is necessary for us to examine the entire question of transmission by satellite. If it is necessary to have a C.B.C. then, I say, the C.B.C. should be charged with the responsibility,^ at this stage of our proceedings, of examining that question. This bill ought to set up the machinery which would guarantee that the C.B.C. will be able to use our space in the near future.
We should reserve Canada's space for Canada. We should share it, rent it or sell it if we do not want it, but we should reserve our right to our space and that space ought to be disposed of in a way which will be good for Canada. Another country should not be allowed to reserve our space; we should not put ourselves in the position of having to go to someone else, hat in hand, asking for permission to use our space.
There are many difficulties to setting up orbiting satellites. We may have the knowhow, but we do not have the resources to do it. I'think that all these questions should be worked out by an agency that ought to be established by the present bill. I do not believe that this bill ought to be amended in one or two years. If it is left in its present form I see no alternative to our coming back to amend it. Should that happen, we shall have been very shortsighted.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a few things only about the broadcasting bill. First, I wish to add my voice to those who have previously spoken in criticism of some C.B.C. productions. I think we should look to some other body than the C.B.C. for productions that are suitable to be televised. Some independent body ought to make these productions and sell them. I am referring to feature films and not to those productions that are made to be released almost immediately, news interviews and so on. Provision ought to be made for some industry which would make films for sale to television operators.


Then, the C.B.C., C.T.V. and other broadcasting networks could buy or rent those productions; in that way, by having available productions which are produced at competitive prices, we should escape the criticisms which are directed at the C.B.C. in connection with its productions. Those criticisms are very serious indeed.
One of my main reasons for rising is that I v/ant to make another plea for the extension of broadcasting facilities in the northern areas of Canada. It is incredible that out of a budget of from $140 million to $170 million we should quibble about the $200,000 to $250,000 which would provide the complete establishment of television facilities throughout the entire northern parts of our provinces.
Hon. members of the house may be surprised at this, but the cost of translators for television broadcasts is very, very minor indeed. You can set up a minor broadcasting or relay station, with a translator, for as little as $3,500. That station can pick up signals from the air. Bear in mind that modern facilities for scrubbing certain signals exist. It has been said to me by engineers that a signal can be transmitted from Vancouver, through a translator, to the Prince George district of British Columbia and that the signal there will be stronger and clearer than the signal which is received by sets in the city of Vancouver from the local broadcasting station.
c (8:50 p.m.)
The reason is that there is a lot of local interference in the city; those who live right in the city do not get as good a signal as that transmitted 500 miles through the relay to the outskirts of Vancouver where there is little interference. This proves that the ability to use translators to bring a signal into the far reaches of the north is ours for the taking, and I emphasize once again that an expenditure of a quarter of a million dollars out of a budget running as high as $170 million seems like peanuts when one considers the result that could be achieved.
The prime purpose of the C.B.C. was to bring broadcasting, whether radio or television, to regions where it would be uneconomic for private enterprise to provide it. This is spelled out in the new bill. I must say I was pleased to receive a letter from the minister in which I was informed it was government policy to give priority to bringing signals to these outlying areas. I must say I am interested in having these signals made available free to all who live in such areas.
January 23, 1368

Why should people in Valemount in my constituency have to make payments every month in order to get television of sorts, in addition to providing funds for the transmitter? It does not make sense. Everyone else gets free television. Think of the millions being spent by the C.B.C. to wean Canadian business away from United States stations. Well, there are people in the north who still do not have transmissions of any kind available to them, though the provision of a signal would involve a paltry sum of between $3,500 and $7,000.
The C.B.C. comes cap in hand asking for a five-year budget as far as operating expenditures are concerned. I cannot find words strong enough to denounce a policy which allows the C.B.C. a five year budget. What in the world is this parliament for if it is not to scrutinize expenditures of this type and see whether or not we are getting value for the money spent? I recall the years gone by when no broadcasting committee was set up and when we were unable to examine the affairs of the C.B.C. in any effective way. I should like to see the broadcasting committee meet every year, with a report from the management before it for discussion as is the case with any other Crown corporation, and the C.B.C. getting money on the basis of its performance.
Nothing could be more appalling than that the government of Canada should even consider allowing a five year budget. There is not a businessman in Canada of any experience who would subscribe to such a thing. Certainly we need some action on the part of hon. members on all sides of this house to make certain that this five year plan is put on the shelf. In this connection, we are all aware that the government is very much concerned today about the rate of government spending. If this state of affairs continues we may have to cut back the $170 million allotted to the C.B.C. as part of a deliberate program. If there is a possibility of getting ourselves into a lot of trouble in the financial world today, why should we put a glorified circle around the C.B.C.?
I, myself, am interested, of course, in plans for an airport terminal at St. George. I agree that if the government is pressed and has to reduce its spending, we shall have to be patient and wait. But why in the world should we wait for the building of an airport terminal there merely to fatten the C.B.C. with multi-millions of dollars in excess of the amount required to bring needed facilities to Prince George and the surrounding area?

When my time expired a short while ago I was referring to the clause in this proposed act which would give the C.B.C. its operating expenditures by means of a five year grant rather than through an annual grant under the present system. It is true we have never received an explanation from the C.B.C. as to how they spend their money. On the other hand, parliament does get an opportunity once a year to find out how much the C.B.C. proposes to spend in the following year, which gives a rough indication of the base they will use to exceed as the 12 months roll by. As I say, we have never succeeded in getting details of the corporation's expenses. Nevertheless, it is my belief that to give the corporation funds on which to operate for five years at a time is a denial of democracy and a mockery of parliament.
Why should we give the C.B.C. its operating budget on a five-year basis and not do the same for the department of defence? We could give the department of defence the money for a unified force in five year grants. We could do the same for the Department of Agriculture. We could give the Department of Trade and Commerce the funds it requires for five years. Then, parliament would not have to meet more than once every five years. I have already pointed out, however, that the annual meeting of parliament is something which dates back into history as far as the passage of the Bill of Rights in 1689, and indications are even further back than that. But in 1968 we find a cabinet in Canada which says it is not necessary to vote funds once a year on an annual basis; the C.B.C. would like to be treated in the same way as the Canada Council and allowed to ask for its appropriation only once every five years.
Do you realize, under the five year plan which is mentioned in this bill, that if the St, Laurent government in say, April, 1957, had given the C.B.C. its funds for five years' operating expenses the Diefenbaker administration, in its term of office from June, 1957, to March, 1958, could have done nothing with the C.B.C., even though it had been elected by the voters of Canada in June, 1957? There is a five year idea behind this suggestion in the bill. I have heard some hon. members
5886	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting state that they cannot go for the five year plan but that they would go for a three year plan. They think a three year plan would be better than a five year plan. But the three year plan would also have covered the entire first administration of the Diefenbaker government, and it would have been unable to do anything with the C.B.C. during its ten months' tenure of office, because the St. Laurent government would have provided five year or three year grants in April 1957.
The first Pearson administration lasted from April, 1963, to November, 1965, a little better than two and a half years. If the three year plan, as suggested, had been in effect it might have been possible for the Diefenbaker administration, in February or March of 1963, to have voted three year's operating appropriations to the C.B.C. and the Pearson administration, in its first term, from April, 1963, to November, 1965, would not have been able to do anything with the expenses of the C.B.C. because the defeated Diefenbaker administration had voted them their three year's funds in, say, March, 1963, prior to the general election when the Diefenbaker administration was turned out of office. How ridiculous can you get?
The three year plan is not satisfactory, but let me give you the most glaring example that would have occurred under this proposed five year operating budget scheme. Under the five year budget operating scheme if the St. Laurent administration in, say, May of 1957 had voted five years' funds to the C.B.C. then the C.B.C. would have been carried from May of 1957 to May of 1962, and we had the first Diefenbaker administration taking office in June, 1957. It would not have been able to do anything with the C.B.C. expenses because the C.B.C. would have been granted five years' appropriation by the St. Laurent administration prior to its defeat in June, 1957.
But worse than that, under the five year proposal contained in this bill, when the hon. Mr. Diefenbaker went to the country in March, 1958, he came back with the largest number of supporters that any party or any prime minister has ever received in the history of Canada-208 Conservative members. In a house of 265 members he had 208 seats. Now, he was in power from March, 1958 until June, 1962, with his second administration, a four year term. Do you realize that if the St. Laurent government under the proposed scheme had given the C.B.C. its five year appropriation, then from June of 1957, when

DEBATES	January 23, 1968
Mr. Diefenbaker formed his first administration, right up to May of 1962, about which time his second administration was expiring, he would never have been able to do a thing with the C.B.C. appropriations despite the fact that in March, 1958, he came into this house with the largest number of supporters in the history of Canada, 208? With a five year appropriation for the C.B.C. passed by the St. Laurent government in May, 1957, the prime minister of Canada and his cabinet would not have been able to do anything with the expenses of the C.B.C. during his first administration from June, 1957, to March, 1958, and for the next four years in his second administration when he had 208 supporters.
What would be the use of holding elections to the House of Commons if the men elected were going to be denied the opportunity of administering the affairs of state? We are told when the budget is brought to us each year that we are in control of only a certain proportion of the total funds. We have a statement made to us that something like 35 per cent of the budget is covered by long-term debt on which we have to pay the interest and some sinking fund payments. Then, we have statutory payments set by law, such as the salaries of judges. All this comes pretty close to 50 per cent of the annual budget which the houses of parliament, the House of Commons and the Senate, cannot touch because those expenditures have been fixed for some time into the future by parliaments of the past. These are expenditures which parliaments have seen fit to take upon their shoulders, knowing them to be right, legal and above board.
If we agree to give the individual arms of government five year budget appropriations, the day will come when the annual budget will not control a single, solitary cent. The C.B.C. will say, "We have got our money for five years." The Department of Trade and Commerce will be wanting similar treatment. The C.N.R. will want similar treatment, and in no time at all the annual budget of parliament will mean nothing because we have committed ourselves to five year grants for spending the funds. This is a situation that cannot be allowed to occur, and this clause in the bill should be changed.
During the consideration of this clause of the bill in the committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts, I moved that we should retain the existing section 35 of the Broadcast Act of 1958 which calls for
January 23, 1988

annual appropriations and, as I have said earlier today and I repeat again, the absence of responsibility is the mother of extravagance.
If the C.B.C. is not going to be required to come to us at least once a year and explain their actions, and explain what they hope to do in the coming 12 months, then parliament should not be meeting at all except on a once in five years basis. It makes an entire mockery of the election of members to parliament if we are not going to have the expenses of the various departments of government submitted to us annually, as has been the practice in Britain since 1689 when the Bill of Rights was passed, a practice which has been adopted in Canada.
When I expressed my opposition to this proposed five year budgetary plan in the House of Commons committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts, a member of the committee gave me the very fast answer that what one parliament has done another parliament can undo, the idea being that if one parliament made a mistake the nex parliament could change it. Now, that is a very nice, glib phrase, that what one parliament has done another parliament can undo.
I would remind you, Mr. Chairman, and members of the committee, that in 1890 the British parliament ceded Heligoland to Germany by an act of parliament in exchange for the island of Zanzibar. I ask, do you think that any British parliament is going to reverse that act of 1890 and regain Heligoland for the British people once more and, in fact, give Zanzibar back to Germany? Anybody can see that glibness is the major characteristic of the phrase "What one parliament has done another parliament can undo." The ceding of Heligoland in 1890 is a good case in point.
Another one is the acknowledgement of the independence of the United States of America. The United States of America rebelled against British control in 1776. The American revolution was settled by the Treaty of Versailles of 1783. Of course the Treaty of Versailles of 1783 had to be ratified by the British parliament. Of course it was ratified by the British parliament, and i6 on the statute books of the British House of Commons to this day. Are you going to tell me what one parliament has done another parliament can undo, because I ask you how are we going to reverse the action of the British parliament that acknowledged the independence of the United States of America when it approved
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting the Treaty of Versailles of 1783, after the American revolution?
We cannot undo in one parliament many things that might have been done by a prior parliament. It would be best if the members of this parliament would bear in mind that parliament can undo what another parliament has done, with limitations, but it would be much, much better if members bore in mind the statement that one parliament cannot bind another parliament. If one parliament could bind the next, why have parliament met annually? Why have parliament elected every four or five years, because if one parliament can bind the next we might as well pass all the necessary laws for the rest of time this winter and never have to come back again to consider changes in the method of living in this country. We can pass laws which we can say will be in effect for the next 75 years. I say to you that no parliament can bind a succeeding parliament. We should not be so puerile as to suggest that any branch of government should be given five years' operating expenses in five year grabs. This is simply an effort on the part of the creature of the federal parliament to get out from under the control of those people who are responsible for taxing the public of Canada in order to maintain the necessary services, of which we consider the C.B.C. to be one.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
I emphasize as broadly as I can that it is ridiculous to ask parliament to bind the parliaments over the next four years to a C.B.C. operating budget. I have already explained how, if this had been in effect in May 1957, the hands of the newly elected Diefenbaker government in June 1957 would have been tied and how the hands of the second Diefenbaker administration in March 31, 1958 would have been tied. What would be the use of holding elections at all? Why ask the people to vote if when the elected representatives get to Ottawa they cannot do anything about the expenses of the government agencies because it has already been agreed that the C.B.C. shall have its money in five year grabs.
I cannot speak against this five year financing of the C.B.C. in any stronger terms without losing my temper. I cannot see how a Liberal cabinet could sensibly and knowingly propose such a denial of democracy as this proposal for a five year operating budget. A five year capital expense budget would be all well and good; that is normal practice. But to
January 23, 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting propose a five year operating budget and asking the parliament of Canada to approve it, thus binding succeeding four year parliaments, is something which is more than human nature can stand. I cannot believe the cabinet has given this matter the consideration it deserves. I sincerely ask that this matter be reconsidered by the cabinet and that a much more sensible proposal be brought in regarding the manner of financing the C.B.C.
When this bill was being considered by the standing committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts the member for Saskatoon but his finger on a troublesome point which I think should be drawn to the attention of the House of Commons at this time so that this matter may be given consideration before the clause by clause study of the bill commences. The member for Saskatoon, Dr. Brand, was discussing clause 19, and his remarks are reported at page 138 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts for November 23. He expressed a lot of concern about the amount of power that can be delegated by the executive committee of the proposed council to one permanent member and one non-permanent member to hold a public hearing and still have all the rights and privileges as pointed out in subclause (7), that are vested in a superior court of record.
The member for Saskatoon went on to say:
It concerns me a little that you are going to have a public hearing held by just two individuals who have these powers which are quasi judicial powers; perhaps even judicial without the quasi, I do not know.
The member for Saskatoon pointed out that he had the impression that the powers were altogether too great to be given to some organization outside of a court of law. He quoted a section and pointed out that the members so designated have, and may exercise for the purpose of such hearing, the powers of the commission set out in subsection (7) which includes all such powers, rights and privileges as are vested in a superior court of record. He went on to say that this includes such things as the enforcement of its orders, the entry of and inspection of property. The hon. member said, "This is the sort of thing which concerns me".
He went on:
Then, if you turn to clause 26 which refers to appeals from such orders, there is reference only to the Commission itself. There seems to be a distinct difference between the Commission and a two-member committee set up by the Commission.


The appeal lies only from a decision of the Commission and not necessarily from a decision of any subcommittee of the Commission that may be set up.
As the hon. member went on to point out, these people have the authority, if this bill is passed in its present form, of a superior court of record. It would appear that they can enter upon property upon their own verdict, having been given powers the same as a superior court of record. This is giving the C.B.C. carte blanche with a vengeance. This is a clause in the bill which should be reconsidered and reworded because there is no reason for confering such powers upon them when the courts of law are established and have been established in this country for many many years.
I have no desire to enter into a discussion of the question of the programming of the C.B.C., as this discussion has been handled by abler persons than myself. I certainly would like to refer, however, to the millions of dollars which are being spent unnecessarily by the C.B.C. in maintaining a national newsgathering organization of its own. I know of no reason that the taxpayers of Canada should be expected to pay for the operation of a national newsgathering organization, not only throughout Canada but also in various parts of the world. This matter was brought before the broadcasting committee where, of course, there was a majority of Liberal members, and we are considering a bill here which has been introduced by a Liberal cabinet.
At that time I pointed out that for something over 65 years we have had in Canada a marvellous newsgathering organization, namely, the Canadian Press. This is a cooperative newsgathering organization consisting primarily of the daily newspapers of Canada from coast to coast. It covers the news as it develops in all quarters of the Dominion of Canada and, through its arrangement with such organizations as the Associated Press in the United States and Reuters in Europe, has a world-wide newsgathering facility. I mentioned that this is a newsgathering service which is adequate for the daily newspapers of Canada. The daily newspapers of Canada have been accepted by the people of this country for almost 100 years as a satisfactory news service, but the C.B.C. cannot be satisfied with such a news service; it must build a news service of its own. Why cannot the C.B.C., in its broadcasting of news, rely on the same service as the daily and weekly newspapers, namely the Canadian Press.
January 23, 1968

The C.B.C. spends millions of dollars building up a newsgathering organization. They have bragged that they would build up a competitive service against the Canadian Press. As I said in the committee and repeat now, the Canadian Press does not buy any news from the C.B.C., but the C.B.C. subscribes to the Canadian Press. That should indicate which is the superior of the two. I cannot express adequately my disgust at the fact that the Canadian taxpayers are being asked to pay, and that taxes are being levied against them to pay, for a competing news service. When I brought the matter before the broadcasting committee I received the smart answer that no doubt when Reuters began to compete with Wolffe and Havas, other newsgathering organizations in Europe, they were protested by the old established organizations. I have no doubt that if someone started up a newsgathering service in Europe in the past both Reuters and Wolffe would have objected. [DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
I have not the slightest doubt but that Wolffe, Havas and Reuters objected one about the other as these newsgathering services came on the scene, but the difference is that they were privately operated organizations battling on even terms. I know of no reason Canadian Press should be asked to compete with a government subsidized and operated newsgathering organization.
I can give many instances of extravagant expenditures by the C.B.C., the worst of course being the recent coverage of the PanAmerican games in Winnipeg. The best information that newspaper people in Canada could obtain is that the C.B.C spent millions of dollars covering this event as compared with the $18,000 spent by the Canadian Press. The expenditure of the C.B.C. newsgathering service in opposition to C.T.V. in Winnipeg would bring tears to the eyes of any taxpayer aware of the tremendous and excessive expenditure by the C.B.C.
I have told you about this in the past but I think it is a wonderful example of the extravagance of the C.B.C. When his Holiness the Pope visited Israel some years ago, the Canadian Press did not send anyone from Canada to cover this historical event. It very satisfactorily relied on the detailed coverage made available by the Associated Press and by Reuters from Europe. Very fine coverage was given in the Canadian press of this visit by His Holiness to Israel. What did the C.B.C. do? They flew two crews to Israel; one French camera crew and one English camera
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting crew as well as English and French commentators. I have asked this question on many occasions but have yet to receive an answer. What difference could there be in the scenery of Israel at the time the Pope visited the holy land as disclosed by a French camera or an English camera, both owned by the C.B.C.? One will have an idea, when he learns that the Canadian Press did not send anyone to Israel at that time but that the C.B.C. sent two camera crews and two crews of commentators, just what little regard the C.B.C. pays to expenses.
Another classic example relates to the uproar that developed in Panama when some Panamanians took some pot shots at some Americans in the canal zone. The Canadian Press thought an adequate coverage of the Panamanian zone uprising would be provided by world wide news organizations and Canadian Press relied on them. The C.B.C. flew people down to New Orleans and to Panama. I ask you what in the name of heaven could the Canadian C.B.C. crew see in the Panama Canal zone that was not adequately reported by the Associated Press people.
I cannot for one moment understand why the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is supposed to be covering all facets of the world scene. As mentioned by the hon. member for Villeneuve during his remarks, I believe, the Canadian Broadcasting Policy should be confined to Canada. If we have some newsgathering we want from all four comers of the world, let us subscribe to the newsgathering services which have covered those corners of the world for members of the fourth estate for a long time, and covered them satisfactorily. We are not adding anything to the enlightenment of the world by sending C.B.C. correspondents to Saigon and South and North Viet Nam, particularly when they come back here and attack the methods of the United States government in conducting that war.
The C.B.C. has been engendering international incidents by flying junior help to Viet Nam who come back and make off-the-cuff statements, embarrassing to the Canadian government and provocative to the United States government, with whom we should at all times be on the friendliest of terms. I know no proper reason for the Canadian broadcasting corporation to send representatives or correspondents to Viet Nam to cover a scene
January 23, 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting that is adequately covered by other newsgathering organizations. The Canadian Press service covers this scene adequately by gathering news from the organizations with which it co-operates.
I hope I made myself clear when I said I could not support a five year operating budget for the C.B.C. I could not care less who introduced the bill in parliament. It will not have my support because of this clause alone.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have been moved to take part in this debate by the remarks of the hon. member for York-Hum-ber. I have never known so many people to be moved by that hon. member's speeches. Let me set straight a fairy story that has been told here during the past two or three hours. It has to do with the suggestion that this house has control over the spending estimates of any department. Where is the hon. member of this house who can remember a time when the estimates of a department have been reduced in this house? I suggest this has never happened in modern history. Surely, this is a fairy story or a myth.
This myth, as described by the hon. member for York Humber, is to the effect that the elective representatives have some control over the government and the C.B.C. As I have mentioned, and as the minister could explain if she were so inclined, the fact of the matter is that the department heads and the president of the C.B.C. decide how much money they need, be it $114 million or more. The estimates then go to the cabinet and to the treasury board. Usually, the treasury board cuts the estimates by perhaps 25 per cent. These department heads and the C.B.C. officials are smart enough to add 30 per cent to their budget needs and they end up better than even.
These estimates then come to the house and are the subject of votes of non-confidence. The rules are such that when the estimates are before the house hon. members can talk about the lumber industry in British Columbia, the fishing and coal industries in the maritimes or anything else they wish. The fact of the matter is that no one talks about the estimates. Finally a member, like that gentleman who is now a feature writer, Mr. Douglas Fisher, moves that the estimates be reduced from $114 million, or whatever they might be, to $1. That usually is the final vote. At no time does it seem that anyone ever questions why the C.B.C. or any other department needs the money it has requested. This whole thing is nothing more than a myth or an exercise.

About the fall of 1964 the committee on parliamentary procedure made a report. At about that time the Prime Minister said in this house he thought it would be a very good idea if departmental estimates were taken out of the house and put into committee. He said that this would give the backbencher and parliamentary committees a certain sense of representative power. He said they could examine these departmental estimates, make recommendations and determine the amounts of money to be made available.
This all sounded very reasonable, because members of parliament could then question the officials of the department as to their money needs. They could also reduce the amounts available to the civil service to carry out these many ventures. If members of parliament had these powers, I am sure a great deal of attention would be paid to what the members had to say. When the amended rules were presented it was obvious that the estimates of the departments may be referred to committees for examination only. The committees can not determine the amount of estimates nor even make recommendations that are likely to be accepted. That is the fact in our parliamentary system.
These criticisms have been placed on the record for the past 25, 30 or 40 years, and I refer to the fact that this house has absolutely no control over departmental spending. We are now asked to approve five year budgeting.
* (9:30 p.m.)
I can see nothing at all wrong with that. In fact, most businesses and enterprises today find it necessary, in order to conduct a good endeavour, to plan five years ahead. I can see nothing wrong with the Department of Finance doing the same thing. In fact, we should be giving very serious attention to making plans over a longer period, say between three and five years, so that business in this nation will know what it is facing, agriculture will know what it is facing and the C.B.C. will know what it is facing. Let us forget this myth, this fairy story about parliamentary control over spending.

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting public property. That is something everyone admits.
Secondly, it is obvious that radio wave lengths are limited and that t.v. channels are even more so. This field of radio and television broadcasting is therefore very limited.
First of all, it belongs to the public. That we have seen. Secondly, it is something that has limits.
I wonder why, in revising its Broadcasting Act, the government did not think of giving the council which will deal with broadcasting in the future the right to have a say concerning the prices charged by these radio and television stations. If, for instance, the Bell Telephone Company wants to increase their rates, they have to prove to the Transport and Communications Board that an increase in prices is necessary. Without such a proof, they will have to maintain the current rates.
The same applies to trucking or railway or air transport companies operating in exclusive fields and wishing to increase their rates.
The trucking company must apply to the Transport Board, railroad or airline companies have to do the same because they are involved in exclusive fields.
Telephone, for instance, is an exclusive field. In front of my house or in front of anybody's house, there is only one telephone line. There are not two. The subscriber has no choice. He is forced to use such and such a line. Other companies are prohibited from coming into the territory of another company. Services are exclusive. In order to protect the subscriber and prevent his being exploited by just one company, such companies, when they want to increase their rates and prices, are required to come before the Transport and Communications Board and prove the necessity of the increase applied for.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, few subjects have been discussed in this parliament so regularly, although recently with an appalling sense of frustration, indeed dismay, as increases in pensions for retired public servants, including the armed forces and
January 23, 1968	COMMONS
the R.C.M.P. Upon no subject has the government been so evasive, so dilatory, so ready to talk out of both sides of its mouth. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 20 last I put the following question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson):
Could he tell the house whether the government intends to finance a publicity campaign from the proceeds of liquor taxes to inform the public of the dangers of alcoholism?
Mr. Speaker, I did not obtain an answer to my question then, because it was ruled out of order. This is why I have asked to discuss it at ten o'clock and, this evening, I hope that I will obtain a satisfactory answer from the representative of the minister, because I think that every member of the house is aware of the harmful effects of alcoholism in Canada.
In 1955, the number of alcoholics in Canada was estimated at approximately 158,000, and according to the figures released for 1965, their number has reached 350,000. This points to an alarming outbreak of alcoholism which has disastrous effects for Canada, first through a lost of efficiency at work and a decrease in the professional output of alcoholics and a general laxity in social conduct.
We also know that excessive drinking largely contributes to traffic accidents resulting every year in many deaths and disabilities. We are aware that it causes considerable loss of time, and what affects everybody, I believe, both alcoholics and abstainers, is the increase in insurance for the protection of motorists. This increase affects everyone and we are indirectly victims of alcoholism in Canada.
On the other hand, we also know that alcoholism brings on all kinds of illnesses filling up our hospitals and our sanatoriums. We also know that, in a large measure, our jails are filled with alcoholic subjects.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
So, Mr. Speaker, for all these reasons, together with the president general of the Association Lacordaire du Canada, I am asking the government to help the groups and organizations fighting alcoholism in Canada.
We know that in 1965 revenue from the sale of alcoholic beverages yielded $281 million to the federal government, and we also know that the same year the federal government had not spent a single cent to fight alcoholism or inform the people on the problems of alcoholism in Canada.
At this stage, I would now like to quote the remarks made by Dr. Charland, president of the Association Lacordaire du Canada, during the national anti-alcoholism week held from November 12 to 18, 1967, as reported in the newspapers:
The time has come for our governments, federal as well as provincial, to ponder the seriousness of the problem of alcoholism in order to draw up a real balance-sheet, that is to say establish clearly what the sale of alcoholic beverages brings in taxes, etc. and, on the other hand, what it costs in medical care, social benefits, loss of time, energy, health, etc. The time has come also for the governments to dip into the millions of dollars they get from the sale of alcoholic beverages to rectify and offset through objective information the noisy campaign now under way to sell those beverages, without neglecting at the same time to bring that advertising back within the limits of common sense and the common good.
Mr. Chairman, these remarks made by Dr. Charland are sensible and I think the government should draw from revenues derived from the sale of alcoholic beverages sums which could be made available to organizations which, everywhere in Canada, are fighting against alcoholism and informing the people on the ill effects of alcohol.
I think that the government should consider favourably representations made by associations, such as Lacordaire and others, requesting grants to help them fight more effectively the harmful results of alcoholism and have people better informed against the use of alcoholic beverages.
We know that distillers and brewers take advantage of advertising to show the bright side of drinking, but we must also show the dark side of the picture so that the public will be well informed.
Therefore, I hope that the government and the officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare will give favourable consideration to this request made by our antialcoholic associations.

January 23. 1968

Mr. Speaker, the Department of National Health and Welfare has no specific program on this subject but it has assisted provinces in a variety of ways for many years. This assistance has included grants for services, for training of personnel and for research studies related to the problem of alcoholism. In addition to this support, and in keeping with the modern attitude which considers alcoholism as a disease and a personality defect, the mental health division has given the subject continuing attention over the years in the following ways:
(a)	Public education. The division has produced a ten page pamphlet entitled "Alcoholism", in both English and French. This pamphlet has been issued for use by the provinces through the health educator and has had rather wide distribution.
(b)	A film, "Profile of a Problem Drinker", sponsored by the Ontario department of health was produced a few years ago through mental health grant funds and professional co-ordination of the mental health division.
(c)	A survey, "Government Programs on Alcoholism", a 90-page study of the activities in some foreign countries, sponsored by the mental health division and prepared by an international authority, the late Dr. E. M. Jellinek.
